That the Parliament of Canada urges the government of the Soviet Union, a co-signatory with Canada of the Helsinki Final Act, to take into account the humanitarian factors involved in these cases and allow Mrs. Nudel and the Slepak family to emigrate to Israel.

Today we see in the papers that the same taxpayer, who controls a Canadian company, is having that company pay him $2.7 million in reimbursement for disbursements he said he made in retaining control of the company. He is a former Canadian citizen now living in Panama and this money is coming from a Canadian company and will be paid to him, although he owes the government $5 million-money which the government has spent ten years doing nothing to collect.
I brought this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister six weeks ago by way of a memorandum, and I have also done so by way of questions in this House. His response has been to laugh it off, to pretend he knows nothing about it, and to pretend it is a matter of no interest to the taxpayers of this country, to the 10 million or 12 million people who pay their taxes every year.
You might be wondering what my question of privilege is, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to speak on this motion for a few moments I am bound to say that, judging by what occurred in the House yesterday and today, perhaps there comes a time when parliament should close and that to keep parliament here might do the institution damage. I see that Your Honour is nodding in agreement. I am happy to see that, because notwithstanding that from time to time there can be difficulties and feelings that perhaps all sides of the House might not agree with Your Honour's rulings, I am going to say to you, sir, that I think you have endeavoured to be fair. This institution demands that of you, but it also demands fairness from all hon. members in terms not only of how they behave but also of what they say.
If the adjournment could mean anything at all, it could mean that perhaps the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), who was involved in an incident yesterday which I could charitably describe only as disgraceful, would go home. Perhaps the minister might be better to stay there, for the purposes of this institution, until he has cooled off and understands that, as we approach a holiday to celebrate our country tomorrow, it might be better if certain things were not said, let alone thought, especially in this institution.
I can only attribute the concern of the parliamentary secretary to the fact that he is overtired from a long session. I want to be as charitable as I can with respect to the parliamentary secretary, with whom it is my pleasure to deal regarding the
June 30, 1978

intricacies of the House of Commons. There is no place in this institution, which has evolved and which has been strengthened over the course of 500 years, for the kind of incident which occurred yesterday and which there seemed to be some desire to pursue today, because this institution will suffer and the country will suffer. Therefore I say to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) that there comes a time when parliament should adjourn, and perhaps this is the time. It is in this context that I want to reflect back for a few moments on why we are here in the first place.
Your Honour will recall that as a result of the actions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) some time ago, in the month of May, the whole country was gripped with the expectation of an election. That was the expectation, and that expectation was fueled not only by statements uttered by the Prime Minister from his place here but also by his activities. Appointments were made. Statements were made at his press conferences, and the country fully expected that there would be an election.
The Prime Minister conducts himself and makes his decisions based on a number of gospels. I am sure of at least two- the gospels of Goldfarb and Gallup. Having conferred with those characters-and I use that term in its most charitable sense-the Prime Minister decided that perhaps it would be better to switch than fight. So parliament stayed on for a while. But why? What was the reason the Prime Minister gave? The House will recall that the Prime Minister was asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) whether he intended to dissolve parliament and call an immediate election.
I think I am paraphrasing that question correctly. The answer of the Prime Minister was as it appears at page 5307 of Hansard. He said:
Mr. Speaker, I think it has been apparent in the House that we are all concerned with the issues with which the Canadian people are concerned, and they want solutions to these problems at this time.
That was an indication that we were staying for some purpose. The purpose was to find solutions to some of the problems affecting the country. What kinds of problems was the Prime Minister talking about at that time? The Leader of the Opposition asked if the Prime Minister would be introducing a new package of economic measures. The Prime Minister's answer was as it appears at page 5307 of Hansard, as follows:
I do not take it that the Leader of the Opposition is suggesting another budget, but other types of economic measures. I can assure him that they will be forthcoming-
Notwithstanding the words of the Prime Minister, since that time there has not been one item of legislation which would give Canadians any reason to believe that the problems referred to by the Prime Minister would be addressed, let alone solved.
The government introduced Bank Act revisions. That legislation was about three years late. Every ten years there is a revision of the Bank Act. The government knew that as early as 1967, when the Bank Act was last revised, yet it could not
Summer Recess
plan its affairs to have the revisions presented to this House on time to pass them into law by 1977.
The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) introduced a package of measures for small business. That package was passed perfunctorily last night by the House of Commons.
It was passed perfunctorily, not because we are at the end of a session but because the measures were so much of motherhood that there was very little difficulty passing them. The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) made suggestions as to how the measures could be improved. Those suggestions had been made before by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek).
Hon. members will recall that at the press conference of the Minister of State (Small Business) the minister sat beside the leader of his party in the National Press Building as he announced those small business measures. The members of the press, who are not businessmen, regarded the announcement as a great yawn. That was their reaction. I looked into the face of the Prime Minister that day on my television tube, and I saw embarrassment over such picayune, minuscule measures being presented to address such a real problem in this country. There has been nothing else since the Prime Minister declined to face up to the electorate. He and his advisers had to face the reality that all Canadians now realize that this is the most inept, the most incompetent, and there are suspicions abroad that it is the most corrupt government in the history of Canada.
Our country has some severe economic problems, and the Prime Minister refuses to recognize that fact. He blithely continues to tinker with the Constitution, on the premise that economic problems will take care of themselves if they are left alone. I have something to say to the Prime Minister with respect to that. Those economic problems will not go away unless there is some affirmative action by this government, which is now here for however long. Unless there is some economic action and some initiatives taken by this government, those economic problems which plague this country, concern its people, affect its future and can alienate its young people, will not be taken away.
Hon. members opposite who shout across this chamber had better take that into account when they go back later today to their ridings because the people of this country want some answers from the government, and those answers are not forthcoming. Our economic malaise can only become worse if no answers are given and if there is no leadership on the part of the government of the day. This government continues to ignore the realities, and one of those realities is that we have become, to the distress of our citizens, business people and working men and women, a second class economy among western economies, and perhaps that is a reflection of the fact that we have a second class government.
The Prime Minister and his cabinet ministers like to use international comparisons to explain away the country's economic problems. Here are some facts that the Prime Minister

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
does not like to quote. For the past two years Canada has had the highest unemployment rate among the industrialized countries and the worst inflation rate in the world. The Economic Council of Canada says that our economy is capable of growing by at least 5 per cent a year. Under this government we have only obtained that 5 per cent rate once in the last five years. When the Prime Minister took office, Canada had the second highest standard of living in the world. Today, under his leadership, it has fallen to the seventh in the world. During the time the Prime Minister has led his government, the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar has fallen to 50 cents. Last year, the government collected $33 billion in taxes, an increase of 350 per cent since the Prime Minister took office.
What did they spend?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: When the Prime Minister took office, the federal government was spending $10 billion a year. That is now the size of our deficit in Canada. It is an indication of the spending of this government. If it were not wasted, if we had not pursued the Les Terrasses de la Chau-diere project, which is a symbol of waste and mismanagement in this country-

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: That is totally untrue.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-that would be one thing. If we had not built the white elephant at Mirabel, that would be one thing. If we had addressed the problems of senior citizens in this country, who are fighting inflation, and used that money appropriately, that would be one thing. But this government has piled waste upon waste, poor management upon poor management, until now it is not only the distress of its citizens it is becoming the laughing stock of every thinking Canadian.
The unemployment rate is over 8 per cent. Over one million Canadians are out of work. Ten years ago the unemployment rate among young people was 7.4 per cent. Now the rate among young people is 14 per cent.
It is the same all over the world.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The backbencher of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook)-
Today is his last day in parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-says it is the same all over the world. This government is inclined to take credit when things are going well. But let things go badly, and the ministers scuttle for cover and blame world conditions, they blame the provinces, they blame the weather, or indeed they even blame the opposition.
Those are the facts. If backbenchers of the Liberal party are speaking up, it is because I think I am beginning to get to them. They are reacting to my comments.
Over the past year Canada lost 100,000 jobs in its manufacturing sector. Yet, in real terms, during the past five years our

imports have been growing twice as fast as our exports. In the last three years our trade deficit totalled $13 billion. That is more than our total trade deficit for the previous 20 years. I am trying to put the figures on the record so hon. members on the other side, from whose comments it is apparent they do not understand the dilemma facing our country and therefore the challenge facing the government, will understand them. I am having some difficulty in getting through to some of them, but I can tell you that there is not much difficulty outside this place, and if any member over there, particularly the hon. member for Halton who is so outspoken from his seat in the backbenches of his party, thinks his constituents do not understand the record of his government, he has another think coming.
A moment ago I said this government was incompetent. Incompetence has become their hallmark. They used to pride themselves on being the great technocrats in the days of C. D. Howe, Gardiner, the lion of Saskatchewan-I see the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) sitting over there- Stuart Garson, the giants of Canadian liberalism, and the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, in times when that party stood for something. I did not agree with what they stood for then as I watched them from the gallery of the House of Commons, but I agreed more with what they stood for then than I agree with what they stand for today. That party stood for something, and one of the things they were supposed to stand for was competence, the ability to manage, the ability to get things done in a reasonable sort of way. All was not perfect, and they would admit that, but they prided themselves on their competence.
Well, in terms of competence, the bottom line expectation of people for their government, how else could one describe the ability of this cabinet when one has to acknowledge that it cannot even deliver the mail? The hon. member for Halton knows that too.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: It is one of the best services in the world.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
During the past ten years the cost of mailing a first class letter has increased from 6 cents to 14 cents. The government has invested several hundred million dollars in automated equipment for the Post Office to make it more efficient, and yet the number of employees in the Post Office has risen from 36,000 to 61,000, and a letter posted in the west end of Toronto has to be sent to Cornwall for processing before it can be delivered to the east end of Toronto.
What has been the government's answer to the Post Office problems? Their answer has been to appoint seven postmasters general in ten years. One of them has become the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Blais). He sits in the House today and he is as distinguished in that post as he was as postmaster general.
The federal government now spends $6 million on telegrams. That just shows how reliable they find the mail. Last night I was trying to find the statistics to point out to the government just how much they have spent on courier service, but I must



June 30, 1978

confess I did not find them. The amounts are tremendous, including the cost of courier service used by the Post Office. This is the measure of confidence that even the casual observer understands. The public is no longer the casual observer with respect to the competence of this government.
The government has about 400 Crown corporations. I say "about 400" because nobody knows for sure. There may have been 387 two months ago, and 1 do not know how many Crown agencies have been created since that time, so I think it is fair to say there are about 400. The list of statistics could go on and on. Surely it must be apparent to the Prime Minister and to everyone that the Prime Minister can no longer ignore reality. The country's economy is in dreadful shape and it requires immediate medicine in order to avoid making the problems even more dangerous, and perhaps in some sectors incurable.
Now I come back to the first point that I made. The Prime Minister has kept parliament here and has stayed away from meeting the people. But the people expected to meet their government on the hustings. The Prime Minister did it because he promised economic legislation on May 11. He has not kept that promise.
Has he kept any promise?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is a judgment that will be made by the public of Canada fairly soon.
Since parliament is in its last day, I will be charitable in my comments respecting the government. Hon. members opposite are beginning to realize that the government, with all its incompetence and questionable practices, is being led by an aging Prime Minister who has lost the confidence of Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The Prime Minister has a government to match him-aging, spiritless, tired, and directionless.
And on its way out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, on its way out. In the Speech from the Throne the government gave lip service to tremendous principles and indicated that great things were to happen. It has given lip service to aiding the private sector. Really it has done more to damage the private sector than any other government in our history.
The government said that it would grapple with and solve the problems of regional disparity. It has done nothing of the kind. If anything, it has exacerbated the problems of regional disparity. The government said that it would make efforts to develop the secondary manufacturing sector of our community where jobs can be found. Instead, we received short-term, make-work programs in place of long-term, permanent jobs. It told the agricultural community that they would be provided
Summer Recess
with a real opportunity. Despite the rising prices of food, the closing of cheese factories and other things, the farmers who work the land still receive a static amount for their produce.
I see the hon. member for Assiniboia is shaking his head. I would like to hear him participate in the debate later. I suppose he can put his case from behind the curtains, if he wants to, but I would prefer to hear him rise and participate at that time. If he feels that milk, pork, lamb, strawberry, apple and tender fruit producers have received a fair shake, in terms of the rising cost of food, then let him present his facts and statistics. They would not be in accordance with the actual facts.
Since 1974, whatever the government has put its hand to, including integrity, has been a failure. During the election campaign in 1974 the government said that it would not touch wage and price controls with a ten-foot pole. Then the government decided otherwise, and that it might be advantageous to do exactly what it said it would not do. That was the beginning of the end of the government's credibility. The government has failed the traditions of its party. It has failed the people it represents, this parliament, in terms of things which are important, and this country. The sooner hon. members opposite are removed from office, the better this country and the world will be.

Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to speak to this adjournment motion, I cannot but note that it is time members of parliament took a well-deserved rest. It is obvious that the work of a member of parliament has become through the years a full-time job and in many respects a most thankless one for those who have to cover long distances to come each week to sit in the Canadian parliament. It is also a thankless job as it is enormously demanding physically for the elected representatives of the Canadian people. It seems obvious to me that in these times of great disruption it would be essential to amend extensively our obsolete parliamentary procedures which were perhaps adequate at the beginning of the Canadian parliament but which no longer meet our present needs nor allow the members of this House to perform as effectively as they would like.
It is obvious that the advent of television in the House has brought to some extent the people closer to what is going on in parliament, since they can see for themselves parliamentarians in action. However when the Canadian people are asked or surveyed about the performance of parliamentarians, at least their performance as seen on television, it is really quite a small part of the daily life of a member. It is unfortunately in many cases a mutilated and unreal image of the enormous responsibilities assumed by parliamentarians, especially on the government side. The question period is telecast mostly throughout the country. Now, you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, to what extent the oral question period enables members of

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
parliament to ask questions and get information on the activities of the government, and especially on the responsibilities of the various government departments. In principle, under our rules, this oral question period should be at the disposal of all parliamentarians on both sides of the House.
Often, for practical, acceptable and understandable reasons, members of the opposition have a much greater share of the oral question period than government members, and in my opinion, this gives a deformed picture of parliamentary life to the Canadian people who are not aware of our parliamentary practice. This is unfair in many respects to the members on this side of the House who cannot ask questions in the House as often as they would like. Second, the duties of a member of parliament go far beyond what happens in the House. For those who work with parliamentarians, and I say this for members of the opposition as well as for the government members, this work goes on for hours and hours in parliamentary committees, in the members' offices, on Parliament Hill, in phone calls to constituents in the various regions of the country, in daily correspondence with many Canadians who ask members of parliament for advice, and of course, in the duty of parliamentarians to return frequently, every week, to their own constituency to meet their constituents, to work at their riding office and better serve the people who have sent us to parliament. Of course, none of this work is shown during the televising of our proceedings. Unfortunately, the Canadian public is not aware of this work, even though it is very important. Now that we are on the point of adjourning for the summer, I feel it is important that the men and women of good will who sit in this parliament take on the responsibility of upgrading our parliamentary procedures and make once and for all parliamentary procedure truly effective.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) would have the people believe that there was not much parliamentary work done in the House and that the government did not proceed as expeditiously as it should with its bills. The facts are quite simple. The truth is that in many cases our procedures are much too slow, we progress at a snail's pace when considering the bills that are introduced and take weeks and even months to pass the bills needed by the people to provide them with immediate services. Parliamentary procedures are such that we can spend many days discussing the principle of a bill. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the second reading stage should be drastically shortened as it is in the British parliament. A bill simply tabled in the House of Commons to determine whether or not it should be further considered by a parliamentary committee should not give rise to more than two or three speeches by each political party represented in the House. There is no need for dozens of opposition members to repeat the same speech. To know if a bill is good or not, if it should be referred to a committee for a clause-by-clause study and to be amended if needed, our procedure should be changed. But the fact that we spend days, months in some

cases, on the second reading of a bill is unacceptable in our modern context. I listened to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who used the adjournment motion to indulge in rhetoric and blame the government for its performance. Of course, I agree that this adjournment motion might give us the opportunity to raise a general discussion on parliamentary activities and particularly on what happens in the House of Commons.
I wish to point out to hon. members a trend that coincides curiously with the advent of television in the House where more and more hon. members feel free to season their questions with lengthy gratuitous statements, half-truths and ludicrous allegations in some cases. And through an abusive use of motions under Standing Order 43, a member can rise at the beginning of the business of the House to make a long statement asking for unanimous consent, to say anything that pops into his mind knowing perfectly well that the motion will not be accepted and that the government will have no opportunity to reply immediately to those gratuitous allegations.
I think that the summer recess should give us the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to review that issue so that hon. members will not be allowed to abuse systematically the parliamentary procedure. I believe it is essential that hon. members on both sides of the House rise only with regard for objectivity and truth which is essential not only for the orderly operation of the House of Commons but also for the people who have now the opportunity to follow our parliamentary proceedings via television and who often hear gratuitous statements that cannot get a forthright answer because of a weakness in our parliamentary procedure. And I believe it is essential in the best interest of public information that we should have a parliamentary procedure ensuring a principle considered essential by the British parliament at the time of its creation, that is fair and equal balance. That check and balance concept is essential in a good parliamentary system. And the check and balance was obviously introduced in the British parliamentary system to encourage to some extent the smaller number of opposition members who, in some cases, at the beginning of British parliamentarianism might have been the victims of an abuse of power by the parliamentary majority. Obviously that check and balance system was established at a time when there were only two political parties. The initiators of that system had in mind the government made up of a political formation and the opposition gathered in another political formation.
Now, with the evolution of the political situation and customs in Canada, there is a proliferation of political parties, so that the checks and balances designed to help the official opposition is also helping the third parties unduly, in my opinion, the small parties which benefit from the same advantages as the official opposition and cumulatively hold an undue and unacceptable margin which had not been intended by those who brought in the checks and balances in parliamentary practice. That is why, as I was saying earlier, our parliamen-
June 30, 1978

tary procedures must be reviewed at all costs, because they are now clearly detrimental to government backbenchers.
