speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of adjournment I recalled the necessity for a reform in the parliamentary procedure, such a reform being necessary not only to enable the backbenchers on the government side to play a greater role in the House of Commons but to reorganize working hours of parliament.
As you know, those working hours are distributed over small time periods in the afternoon and scarcely a few hours in the evening five days a week whereas they could be reorganized and concentrated over four days a week only so that we could
Summer Recess
work longer hours in a four-day week whereas presently we have a five-day week. Of course, this would enable hon. members who come from the ends of the country to go back to their constituency every weekend, they would not be forced, as is now the case for some hon. members from British Columbia, to travel all day long on Saturday to arrive late in the evening in their constituency and to leave on Sunday to come back for Monday for parliamentary business. This is an unacceptable situation which should be revised as soon as possible. Parliamentary procedure should also be amended in order to limit the length of speeches in certain debates.
There is no question of preventing members from expressing their views in this House when they feel they should do so, but in the U.S. Congress there is provision for congressmen, where they are prevented by certain procedures there from delivering their speeches, for tabling them with the clerk of the House, and they are printed in the U.S. congressional record. Such an approach, such a procedure of course would have clear benefits in this House.
Further, parliamentary procedure should be reorganized to establish a reasonable legislative timetable under which the government could have its legislation go through within a justifiable and adequate time frame. It is totally unacceptable that we should live with the current parliamentary procedure wherein legislation sometimes takes two or three years to go through parliament. Such a situation cannot be tolerated. It is mostly, if not entirely, due to the opposition constantly abusing parliamentary procedure to cause undue delays. In my view, Mr. Speaker, it should be provided under a legislative timetable that a bill could not be debated for periods over four months, whether in this House or in committee. Once that period was over we, as legislators charged with the clear duty of enacting statutes, should stop discussing, divide on and pass them.
Finally, I would like to say that apart from and beyond parliamentary reform, the parliamentary spirit needs to be improved. There is matter for concern in the attitude of some members in terms of parliamentary spirit. It will be remembered that some years ago, when I was an hon. member's assistant rather than a member in this House, because I worked in Canadian parliament not on the floor but for a minister of the Crown, I remember very well what happened. I remember the insidious, reviling and malicious attacks against two ministers from Quebec, the hon. Mr. Tremblay and the hon. Mr. Favreau, and I must say that most certainly those cowardly, invidious and unfair attacks mainly contributed to the premature deaths of those two former French-Canadian ministers, highly competent and perfectly honest men. I thought that time was over and that we would not hear any more of that kind of insidious, mischievous and unacceptable attacks in the House of Commons.

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
Yet I cannot help but deplore the fact that we have seen reappearing some kind of Don Quixote who, mischievously and insidiously . .. Perhaps not in certain cases, because we are not supposed to impute motives to members in the Elouse, and this I do not want to do, but I am wondering very seriously about the attitude shown by some hon. members who are trying to spot big black clouds in the Canadian political sky and who, by coincidence, launch unfortunate attacks against certain senior officials, certain cabinet ministers and certain Canadian businessmen in a systematic and deplorable way in my opinion; under the guise of questions, they make gratuitous statements, uttering half truths and odious insinuations in trying to prove that there has been or could have been scandals surrounding the government. Again a few moments ago, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) rose to make a speech: he is the one who, before the lunch break, spoke and said that this government was, and 1 quote, a corrupt government. That is a gratuitous statement without any substance-
Shame!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
This government in power under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for ten years has had none of its senior members convicted of corruption or involved in scandals. An attempt was made to have us believe there were scandals in certains cases; all sorts of questions were put in an effort to stir doubts in the minds of the people. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the ruling given yesterday by a Quebec court acquitting Senator Giguere was an eloquent example of the unfortunate insinuations made by some hon. member of this House of Commons against the authorities of the Canadian government, to try and destroy them in the public opinion, and that without basis, without reason.
I cannot imagine what torment Mr. Louis Lapointe, a Montreal businessman, went through; he was held in high esteem and respected by his peers and he died suddenly as a result of the backwash of the Sky Shop incident. I have no idea to what extent his health was affected by it, but obviously no parliamentarian can or must at any time use his parliamentary immunity to make insinuations or statements lightly, without basis then to hide behind his parliamentary immunity, the privilege of members of parliament, and argue his good faith and simple wish to know a bit more about government operations. That is hypocrisy or irresponsibility of the most serious nature. And I think that as members of this House of Commons, we have a duty to have the highest standard of integrity and the deepest concern for objectivity and impartiality when we are asked insidious questions which may eventually endanger people's reputations and reflects adversely upon their integrity.
Mr. Speaker, earlier the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has charged the government with bad management or incompetence. Well, I shall tell him this: I listened to him very carefully and when he was asked to bring in facts,

the only two cases which came to his mind were les Terrasses de la Chaudiere and the Mirabel Airport, those are the only two cases he mentioned, and they are, through coincidence of course, both located in the province of Quebec.
I know that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton does not like the fact that the Canadian governmnt has erected federal buildings on the Hull side, that the Canadian government is respectably and honorably present on both sides of the Ottawa river, that the National Capital Commission, for the sake of Canadian unity, made sure that federal civil servants would work on both sides of the river, on the Ottawa as well as the Hull side, whatever objections the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton may have, that decision of the Canadian government is irrefutable, it is there and we shall stay on both sides. What is at stake is the unity of the country and an equitable representation of federal civil servants who may work in the national capital and who may serve the Canadian government as well if they work in Hull as if they work in Ottawa. I am not impressed by the big eyeglasses or the big artificial smile of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, his comments cannot be erased, they are very clear and they do not deceive us. He does not like the fact that les Terrasses de la Chaudiere are built on the Hull side, he does not like the fact that there are federal buildings in Hull and he is nit-picking to try to find a so-called scandal which does not exist. And yesterday, when the hon. member for Central Nova asked questions about this matter, les Terrasses de la Chaudiere, he once again, as he has often done in this House, quoted papers he had in his possession heaven knows why, internal confidential papers of departments, government bodies, confidential documents he uses in this House by referring to only a very small portion and leaving the impression that improper transactions took place between the Campeau corporation and the government of Canada.
Well, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to say that those transactions were duly examined and approved by the National Capital Commission on August 12, 1975, and if the hon. member had not quoted those papers only in part, if he had quoted them in their totality, he would see that the design committee of the National Capital Commission approved that project in a letter dated August 12, 1975. The hon. member is wrong in suggesting, as he did, that this project was rejected on several occasions in the months of May, June, July, September and November 1975. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) is wrong, and it is also untrue, as some opposition members seemed to suggest, that the chairman of the National Capital Commission threatened to resign if that project was accepted. That is absolutely false. I personally telephoned the former chairman, Mr. Gallant, to check up on that story and he confirmed that at no time had he threatened to resign, on the contrary, that the Government of Canada had considered that project, recognized the usefulness of having another federal building on the present site of les Terrasses de la Chaudiere
June 30, 1978

and that private contractor had been asked to submit bids that were acceptable and competitive, which was done.
It is rather odd to see, Mr. Speaker, that when the hon. member for Central Nova or other opposition members talk about federal buildings in the national capital they do not talk about those that are already in existence, that were built by other private contractors-Olympia York, for example, or Cadillac Fairview-who like Campeau corporation have what is called a lease purchase plan which was negotiated in all good faith, all honesty, with the government of Canada, just like Campeau corporation negotiated with the government of Canada. And I do not accept that members should under the cover of parliamentary immunity try to imply that there was an injustice, that there was a scandal in that business. It is absolutely unacceptable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Repeat it in English so they will understand!
Say it to them in English.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think I should repeat this in English. It is an unacceptable situation when members on the other side are not responsible enough to lay a charge and completely explain their accusations. Instead, they take advantage of the immunity of this House to make irresponsible charges and allegations, citing unrelated events, telling half truths, presenting only portions of documents, and distorting the real facts.
It is unacceptable that in some cases they endeavour to fabricate scandals not in existence. In so doing they are not only being extremely unfair to those directly involved, but to the Canadian people who get a distorted view of the facts. This unacceptable situation has been going on for too long with some members of the opposition. It should cease.
If we take an adjournment period this summer, we should take advantage of it to redraft our parliamentary procedures no longer to allow those members who have no courage to abuse the rules of this House and its immunity to make all kind of unfounded charges and accusations.

I think that the Terrasses de la Chaudiere issue, which was raised earlier in today's debate by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) was dealt with extensively by a Senate committee which examined all transactions. Moreover, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that representatives of both the Progressive Conservative and Liberal parties participated in these Senate discussions and it was clearly established by the Senate committee that nothing improper was done in that situation, that it was a 100 per cent regular transaction which did not deserve the kind of muck-raking that some members of this House enjoy doing to arouse the interest of the population by raising inappropriate questions on this issue. I would like to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by going over some of the criticisms voiced against the efficiency of this government by
Summer Recess
the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, who says that the government has a poor economic record to show. It seems obvious to me that his speech was written along the lines of a certain electoral platform that the Progressive Conservative party could defend during an election campaign. To me, it sounded more like an electoral speech than a speech on an adjournment motion.
1 think some of my colleagues in this House who will be dealing more thoroughly with those issues after me this afternoon will elaborate on the exceptional achievements of this government in recent years. There is no doubt that this government took whatever steps were necessary to curb the kind of galloping inflation we had in this country. There is no doubt that this government through its Minister of Employment and Immigration, the hon. Jack Sydney George Cullen, created a considerable number of jobs in Canada in recent years, a record number of job opportunities well above the number of jobs created in any industrialized country in the world. The government introduced in recent weeks a series of measures dealing with the support the Government of Canada wants to give small businesses in this country.
We know how necessary and essential small businesses are to the smooth operation of this country's economy, to the creation of jobs not only in large centres but especially in the more isolated areas of Canada. And small businesses are undoubtedly the way to ensure that constant reserve of job opportunities that the people of this country need in order to keep on living even in the remotest areas of this country, and to stem that continuing shift towards larger cities. The government has managed to introduce a whole series of measures to help small and medium-size businesses. We also recently announced a series of measures to help research in Canada, to help industries and universities, particularly those doing scientific research in Canada, create jobs for researchers in this country, to allow our society to progress in the area of research and allow the people of this country to have an even better standard of living.
And, finally, one cannot help but point out the recent efforts made by the Canadian government to have a Canadian constitution written by Canadians for Canadians and a constitution that would truly be ours, that would be patriated and would be a truly Canadian constitution that would fully meet the aspirations of the people of this country. So there you have in the little time I have at my disposal what the government has done as we get ready to adjourn for the summer. We have an extremely enviable record and the people of this country, in spite of the difficulties they might come up against, have one of the highest standards of living in the world. And the people of this country, despite the sombre, negative, pessimistic feelings of the opposition, are very happy to have the opportunity to live in a country called Canada.
Mr. Speaker, during the present session, we have witnessed a pitiful performance by the official opposition, a performance

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
totally inacceptable and unqualifiable by the Progressive Conservative party, a party which has associated itself with phony bugging, with the appointment of private detectives to keep the activities of members and ministers of the government under watch. It is an attitude absolutely intolerable from a supposedly responsible Canadian party. When by-elections were held in the province of Quebec, that party also attempted to make a cozy deal with the Parti Quebecois in order to beat the liberals in Quebec province.
The Progressive Conservative party, which represents the official opposition, has, through its irresponsible actions done more for the destruction of Canada than its unity. Their attitude is wrong, Mr. Speaker, since, as I have said before, the abuse the parliamentary procedure to make allegations and declarations of all kinds, which are not even always correct, hoping through this strategy to cast doubt and confusion in the public mind, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that despite all the sordid stories made up by the official opposition, the Canadian people will make the right assessment when the time comes, of the positive and practical measures toward national unity and prosperity taken by this government, headed by the right hon. Prime Minister Trudeau, leader of the Liberal Party of Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of trying to match the oratory or the rhetoric we have listened to for the last little while. I must say I marvel at the latitude which seems to be provided by a simple motion calling for the adjournment of the House from June 30 to October 10. I would think that this was what we should be discussing, but the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) apparently feels he can raise any matter he wishes to deal with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: What about Baker's speech?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
I have no intention of getting into this quarrel between the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and members of the official opposition, but I suspect we have not heard the last of this discussion. In fact I begin to wonder whether we shall adjourn today after all.
Neither do I intend to use this motion as an occasion for discussing parliamentary procedure but I should like to make a few brief comments on what the minister had to say in this area. I take second place to no one in being concerned about reforming the procedures of this House. I have taken part in many of those reforms, some of which I am proud but others of which we cannot be so proud. There are still improvements which we must make, but I reject completely the suggestion that reform of parliament means reducing debate and reducing the amount of time we spend here so that members will not lose their health serving their constituents for so long in Ottawa.

At election time every candidate promises he will give all he has got to serve the people. Then we hear speeches here such as we just heard suggesting we should limit the amount of time we spend here. There are reforms in our procedure which must be achieved, and we must take this question seriously, but I suggest the speech we have just heard is no blueprint for proper reform.
Having said that I deplore this time being used to discuss matters which are far from the terms of the motion, I shall use the few minutes I wish to take to say something about that motion. The proposal is that we adjourn today, Friday, June 30, until Tuesday, October 10. I quite agree that it is time for this House to adjourn.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
That has been true for quite a while, particularly since May 11. The debates which have gone on in the House since that date have not been a credit to the institution. Indeed, the things which have gone on during the last few days make it clear we ought to get out of here. I think we should do so not only because of the tone of debate in the last little while but because it does make sense for us to have a break from work here, for personal reasons, and so that we can do some thinking about what we ought to put our minds to when we come back. But though I support the idea of a recess I say quite frankly that a recess of 100 days is unreasonable.
We were told on May 11 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that there are many problems which must be resolved-that is the reason the election was put off; it was because parliament could serve the country better by staying here and dealing with legislation. I find it quite inconsistent for the government of the same Prime Minister to propose now that we take a recess of three months and 10 days, or a total of something over 100 days. I believe that at the very least we should be coming back in September to try to cope with the problems facing this country.
I realize we do not know what is in the mind of the Prime Minister. There are all sorts of rumours and guesses about an election. I suspect he has not made up his own mind yet. I realize that the proposal that we come back on October 10 might be set aside by the calling of an election. Then again, the Prime Minister might put off calling an election until some time in 1979.
He might invoke the War Measures Act and not have an election.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Well, that is a suspicion not to be dismissed out of hand. One of the rules of this House is that we are supposed to take each other's word. On the assumption that this motion means what it says and that we shall be coming back on October 10, I should like to make a few suggestions as to what I think the government should be putting its mind to while we are away.
June 30, 1978

I assume that if we carry out the terms of this motion and come back on October 10, that will probably be the date upon which the third session of this Thirtieth Parliament will be prorogued, with the new one being commenced later that day or on Wednesday, October 11.
I shall not take the time of the House to review the past session. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) did a bit of that this morning, and if my leader had not got involved in something else this afternoon he might be doing it right now. But I must say I find the accomplishments of this parliament under the government in the past session very disappointing. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs blames this on the length of time it takes to debate certain matters. He says there are services which the government is prepared to offer to the people which the people are not getting because we debate legislation for so long. What services, Mr. Speaker? The things the people are not getting from this parliament are the things which are not placed before parliament by the government which has the authority to bring in the appropriate legislation.
No one will be surprised by the kind of legislation about which I am concerned. I mentioned one aspect this morning in a motion I sought to move under Standing Order 43. I say seriously to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) and to the government: resolve this problem during the 100 days of the recess. I refer to the pension rights of veterans' widows especially in cases where the veteran's pension was below 48 per cent. This issue has been around long enough. The number of those who might have benefited from proper legislation and who have died, is considerable, and as time goes by more and more veterans whose pensions are below 48 per cent must face the fact that they are growing older and that if they die first there will be no pension for their widows. As a matter of fact, the vast majority of our veterans on disability pensions have pensions below 48 per cent, and they are affected by this rule.
This may not be a subject for the kind of rhetoric and oratory we have had thus far, but I suggest it is a serious issue, and I plead that in this 100-day recess which we are being asked to agree to this afternoon the government give its attention to the problem of providing pro rata pensions for the widows of veterans where the veterans' pensions were below 48 per cent.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
We have also had assurance of the Minister of Veterans Affairs that a thorough study is being made of the War Veterans Allowance Act. This is a piece of legislation which has done a lot of good. It has been around for 47 or 48 years, but times have changed. It was introduced in the days when the old age pension was payable only at age 70-a very small amount and on a means test- and the war veterans allowance was something a little better than that for veterans. Surely the same principle should apply
Summer Recess
now. There should be something a little better for veterans than is available generally under old age legislation today.
I find it difficult to accept the proposition that this kind of study takes months and months and years and years. The matter has been studied already in the department, says the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Now there is this 100-day period.
I think that in the fall the minister should bring in not only a report of that study but also revisions to the War Veterans Allowance Act, making it something much closer to a guaranteed annual income for our older veterans.
I want also to urge that serious attention be given by the government during the next 100 days to a number of other pension matters. I find it unacceptable, to use a word we heard a while ago a number of times, for the government to think that it has done all it should for our senior citizens simply because it has the pension up to a certain point and indexes it in accordance with the rise in the consumer price index. The fact is that with that rise always behind, with the base not having been high enough to begin with, and other conditions which I need not take the time to spell out, the conditions faced by our senior citizens are getting relatively more difficult.
We have watched with interest the sittings of the Royal Commission on Pensions which have been held in the province of Ontario, and I think the interesting thing has been the number of briefs which have been presented to that commission pointing to the difficulties and problems being faced by older people. It is not enough for the government to sit there, complacently saying it has done this and that and that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should hold his peace. Not so. 1 plead that something be done and that it be done during this 100-day period particularly about the position of persons between 60 and 65 years of age, particularly women in that age bracket.
It becomes more and more clear that one of the most cruel and unfair pieces of legislation we ever passed was the spouse's allowance. It is fine for those who get it, a limited number, but in terms of discriminating against women and men, but mostly women, of single status, whether they be widows, spinsters, divorced or separated, I know of nothing which has been worse. The government is finally admitting-the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has said this in public speeches-that it does seem unfair where a person is getting the spouse's allowance-because she is a spouse-and loses her husband before she is 65, that her allowance and her pension are cut off.
I gather from things which have been attributed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in her speeches outside this House that the government is disposed to correct that situation. That is not enough. The whole position of persons between 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market, who do not meet the marital test and so forth, is a difficult one, and this is not something to be left to a campaign issue for the next election. This is not something to be left for the government which takes over after the next election. This is something to be dealt with now.

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
I am taking this motion at its face value. I am taking it for what it says, namely, that we are coming back on October 10, and if we are coming back on October 10 that means there will be another session of this thirtieth parliament. I say that the time to deal with this problem which faces women in particular between the ages of 60 and 65 is early in that fourth session of this thirtieth parliament.
Having made reference to the spouse's allowance and its unfairness to women of single status between the ages of 60 and 65, I want to stress, as I have tried to do on every possible occasion, the unfairness of our pension rules generally as they affect women. There is discrimination against veterans' widows where the 48 per cent rule applies. There is discrimination under the spouse's allowance. There is discrimination under the Canada Pension Plan in that the woman who works outside the home can be part of the Canada Pension Plan and get the benefits of it, but the woman who works in the home gets no such benefit, even though we received a report from Statistics Canada a few days ago which told us that the work which is done in the homes of Canada by the housewives of this nation is worth $80 billion a year, roughly 40 per cent of the gross national product. Yet for most of them there is nothing in terms of the Canada Pension Plan. They get old age security the same as others, but we keep hearing talk about equality.
We get into the question of regions. We get into the question of languages. There are two languages in this country, so we have to treat them equally, and I agree, but there are also two sexes in this country, and I think there should be equality of treatment. If we are not yet prepared to establish that equality all along the line, at least we should establish it when it comes time for retirement and pension.
I am making this short speech directly in relation to the motion. The motion calls for a 100-day recess. I think 60 or 70 days would be plenty. It would be better for us to come back in September, but just as we are being given 100 days to think about these things and to attend to our responsibilities here, in our constituencies and about the country, I contend that the government has a responsibility to look at the things which ought to be done in the next session of parliament.
I think that this last session has been a failure. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs can argue this and take opposite views and all the rest of it. I think the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is much closer to the facts than the Minister of State for Urban Affairs because this has been a disappointing session. Let us not have another one before an election.
I do not think that parliaments which go five years are very successful. I was here in one of them some years ago, and I remember how useless that fifth year was. After four years have gone by it is time to get a fresh mandate, but let us not be hamstrung by that tradition and by that convention. If we are going to come back and have a new session, let us deal with some of these urgent problems.
I press very strongly that the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare use these

100 days to the best possible advantage, and that when we come back in October and start a new session they bring in legislation to provide better conditions for our veterans, their families and all our older people, but especially for the section of our older community which suffers the most, namely, our older women.
There are many other issues which must be of concern to us in the new session which, supposedly, we will have when we come back. My leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), and others of my colleagues have been pressing these points time and time again. These other issues underline the pension issues I am talking about. Something must be done soon to cope with the serious problem of the unemployment of over one million of our people who are not able to find jobs. Unless something is done about this problem, as well as about rising prices which now give us figures of 10 per cent, 11 per cent or 12 per cent a year, the possibility of this country maintaining its unity, its integrity, and the confidence of our people becomes very slim. So, as I have called on the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare to use these 100 days to advantage in their areas, I call on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), and others who have to do with economic policy, and ultimately on the Prime Minister, to regard these 100 days not just as a holiday, not just as a time when they are rid of parliament and all the nasty questions and debates they have to face here, but as a time to do something about creating jobs and coping with inflation so that the economy of this country does not get completely out of hand.
I say again, sir, that we are prepared to support the motion in the sense that it says parliament should take a recess. There is just no argument about that, and the debate today is probably proving the point, but I insist that it ought not to be for 100 days, it ought to be until some time in September after the school term commences. I think that might be a good time for us to come back. But since that is not the case, and if it has to be the 100 days, let the government come back in the fall ready to go into a session on a serious-minded basis, and in particular to have legislation ready to cope with the problems of our veterans, the problems of our senior citizens, the problem of unemployment, and the problem of runaway prices. These things must be done.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to mention that, in spite of the undue length of certain debates which took place in the course of the current session, we were still able to pass several bills. We can indeed look at the relatively positive record of this session and realize that nearly 40 bills were adopted over the last nine months. Some of them of course were of social and judicial nature, for instance the
June 30, 1978

important legislation which will allow every Canadian to be judged before the courts of this country in the language of his choice, whichever official language he uses. We need only to remind hon. members of the legislation we have passed, to promote the basic right of Canadians to work in sanitary conditions, and the many amendments we have brought to the Criminal Code, in particular those which clarify the definition of rape and sexual assault in order to prevent abuses in these kinds of crime.
However, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will remember that in the Speech from the Throne last October, the government established two main lines of priorities, economic and constitutional. As far as economic priorities are concerned, we have of course taken an approach which is different from the one we took on constitutional issues. We have taken several economic measures by passing a large number of bills. I am thinking more particularly of Bills C-l 1, C-15, C-16, C-18, C-19, C-23, C-25, C-29, C-30, C-31, C-38 and C-56, to name only a few, which related to economic measures and which have been considered, passed and received royal assent.
When we discussed constitutional matters, the government showed its leadership in a different way. The government has tabled two bills and a white paper and has set up a Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, in the hope of meeting two specific objectives. First, to allow for a complete, valid and serious consultation of all interested parties, and second to proceed with a constitutional reform, which would lead to a new federalism within a predetermined and reasonable period. The government's approach on constitutional matters as mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, is to tabling the bill respecting referendums, which provides for public consultation of Canadians on constitutional matters. Still more recently, we have tabled a momentous bill, Bill C-60, which aims at a major reform of our federal institutions such as the Senate, which would become a House of the Federation, the Supreme Court of Canada, the authority of the Governor General of Canada and so on.
Moreover, we have tabled a white paper entitled A Time for Action, which contains the major principles for the renewal of the constitution, the real milestones for a renewed federation with a well defined time frame: July 1, 1979 for reforms dealing with strictly federal matters. Of course, this will not prevent consultations with the provinces or other interested parties. We all know that the ministers for federal-provincial relations will have the opportunity to meet during the summer and that subsequently the provincial premiers will meet with the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada for an important conference on constitutional matters. As far as the second term, July 1, 1981, is concerned that is the time we shall need to enter into agreements on distribution of powers, and on the patriation of the constitution and the amendment formula thereto.
Summer Recess
That is in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, a very reasonable approach taken by the government during this session to deal with constitutional priorities. Whereas on the one hand, we have on the economic level, adopted a very large number of programs to boost the economy in this country, we have on the other hand, on the constitutional level, tabled legislation and a white paper to ensure that this reform be made by way of valid and serious consultation and within a specific and reasonable time. And this summer, this joint committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons will seek the views of the public and all those concerned and look fully into the proposals contained in Bill C-60 as well as in the white paper, A Time for Action, and hopefully, report to parliament as early as next fall so that we can bring about the constitutional reform and provide Canadians with a renewed federalism within the time-frame specified in the white paper.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as can be seen, this is a positive record for a session that has lasted for some nine months and during which, as I said earlier, about 40 bills were passed. What I find unfortunate is that bills which were introduced before Christmas, including at least eight which were very important, and other bills introduced before Easter, of which seven were very important in our opinion, could not go through the three readings and receive royal assent. 1 am thinking particularly about Bill C-6, concerning Canadian ports, Bill C-7, which would have removed a lot of bothersome red tape for small businesses, Bill C-l3, concerning combines investigations, Bill C-l4, which concerns nuclear controls, Bill C-20, concerning the disposition and development of oil and gas rights, Bill C-24, concerning telecommunications in Canada, and there are many more, Mr. Speaker. I find it unfortunate that the present parliamentary system, under our present rules, has not allowed us to pass bills such as those I have just listed and, which could have been very useful to the Canadian people. I fully agree with the previous speaker, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), when he advocated an early parliamentary reform.
Mr. Speaker, when we see the grievances of hon. members, and I am referring not only to government members but also to members of the opposition, I believe that the main grievances can be summarized in seven particular areas. Members generally complain about the unwarranted repetition in the House of the same arguments; they complain about speeches that often smack of political partisanship instead of being valid or constructive criticism, which results in too many speakers straying from the main subject; the third most frequent grievance, Mr. Speaker, concerns the abusive use made by the opposition of the time and the means at its disposal during the various stages of the bill in an often admitted attempt to prevent or delay unduly the passage of these bills by the government even though it has a majority. The fourth grievance, Mr. Speaker, is the aberrant constraint of a constant

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
attendance which is too often useless in the House of Commons and which prevents the sound planning and carrying out of the various duties of a member of parliament.
The fifth most frequent grievance is that we have an unmanageable and overly extensive parliamentary program which actually prevents a member from spending valuable time with his constituents and family. Mr. Speaker, we could list other grievances, but I believe that those I have mentioned give a good idea of the state of mind of most members who seek some changes in order to make this House more efficient, more relevant and better able to meet the aspirations of Canadians.
Under the type of reform that we favour, we are of course willing to respect certain principles which boil down to three points that are fundamental in my opinion. Obviously, the opposition has the right to express its views fully but without filibustering, Mr. Speaker. Filibustering has no place in the Canadian parliament. The opposition should be entitled to put forward its views fully without resorting to filibustering tactics, which would remove any opportunity for repetition at the various stages of the legislative process and make for relevant and better speeches. The second principle to be recognized in any parliamentary reform would be to rationalize the attendance of the member in the House of Commons so as to enable him to plan his work and use his time more sensibly. And finally, the third principle to follow in any parliamentary reform would be to set up an orderly parliamentary schedule which would allow a member more time to attend to his parliamentary duties outside Parliament Hill and lead a more normal family life.
Mr. Speaker, if we want to deal with the grievances voiced by most members about parliamentary procedure while abiding by the above-mentioned principles, it would be possible to amend our rules to the satisfaction of all parties.
Of course, it is very difficult to effect major changes with the unanimous consent of all members of a House such as ours, and at times we have to be realistic and make important changes through government bills. I make no secret of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that for my part, I am willing to continue negotiating those necessary changes, to modernize our parliament and make it more efficient with members of the opposition, but I am also willing, if needs be, if such negotiations fail after a reasonable period of time, to urge the government, after recommending and suggesting it, to legislate the matter and allow a reasonable debate in the House of Commons and so allow the Canadian people who, through television, can now watch us, to see a production that is far more decent than that we have been giving them for the last nine months, when we discuss bills and various other topics. A while ago, we heard remarks concerning the attitude of opposition members towards the motions presented pursuant to Standing Order 43, for instance; in that case, the procedure is abused, as we have seen during this session; an attempt is made, above all else, to put forth long partisan and political preambles rather than to

bring the government to state its views on serious matters for the benefit of the Canadian public.
Well, Mr. Speaker, such abuses should be checked and stopped. During the question period, we often see members of the opposition-who indeed have the right to inquire and criticize the government on its administration-abuse this right and attempt to disparage others constantly and systematically, whether parliamentarians, high officials or ordinary citizens involved in public affairs. I suggest that they should not take advantage of their immunity to attack Anglophone or Francophone ministers, members of parliament, businessmen, judges and so on.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that such abuses are unacceptable. The atmosphere of this House must change if we want to set an example for the Canadian people. We have been saying for many years that attitudes should be changed in this country in order to promote a better understanding between our two main linguistic and cultural communities and true equality between our two communities, and I feel that the best example we can set is by changing our own attitude here in the House of Commons. If hon. members showed one another more mutual respect, Mr. Speaker, if they were more honest, if their speeches were not so partisan, if their criticisms were aimed more at policies than at individuals, I think we would be setting for the rest of Canada a fine example of a possible understanding between people of different opinion.
This would be a great change to show through television to our Canadian fellow citizens who watch us and who very often think, and rightly so, that we act like buffoons in this House, Mr. Speaker. We have 40 minutes to talk about various subjects. Most often members have 40 minutes to talk about a bill, and this for nearly all stages of consideration of a bill. This is unacceptable. It is a ridiculous loss of time in 1978. If we have something intelligent to say, if we have a point to make, it seems to me that we could very well do so in 15 or 20 minutes, Mr. Speaker, and the first major change that I would suggest for practical purposes would be to limit the length of speeches to 15 or 20 minutes. Even this would help restrict the debates to the subjects being discussed and ensure more effectiveness in parliament, and it would also be fairer and more equitable. A greater number of the 285 members that we will have after the next election would have the opportunity to speak about various subjects and express their views.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to place my intervention on parliamentary reform in the context of Canadian unity. I have talked about the constitutional legislation that we have presented during this session. I have just talked about the need to set an example by our attitude to promote better understanding and true equality between our two major communities, and I believe that it is important and timely to emphasize this aspect during the debate on a motion to adjourn the House.
June 30, 1978

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that, in general, my experience as parliamentary secretary to the government House leader has been interesting. It has enabled me to see to what extent I was right to complain about our rules and it is urgent to make these changes. It has enabled me to see also to what extent in negotiations to expedite the proceedings of the House, certain people can sometimes be petty and prevent us hypocritically to reach valid and honest objectives for the people of Canada. I cannot congratulate everyone with whom I have discussed or negotiated. However, several of them, and I want to make this clear, have acted in good faith and in a climate of honest co-operation. In the same spirit, I want to thank sincerely-I shall name only one so that some people do not feel uncomfortable-but I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who, given his knowledge of our Standing Orders, has always been frank and honest with me and has helped us go forward in a progressive way. I think his advice has been judicious and we should pay tribute to him in this debate. I would like it if in the future, when we schedule the legislative program of a session, we were able to depend on and believe in the word we are given.
I would be happy if we were always in a position to plan our legislative work in such a way that, when we go back to the people during recess, we do not have anything to say about our opponents' parliamentary spirit. I complained about our Standing Orders, my colleague the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) complained about the parliamentary spirit in this House. Unfortunately in some cases I have witnessed, I must also regret that certain members of the opposition abused, as I said earlier, some procedures. I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to rise on a question of privilege in my concluding remarks, but comments like those made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), who just came into the House, are in my opinion unacceptable in a place like this. It seems to me that the House leader of the official opposition could have refrained today from describing this government as the most corrupt he and Canada have ever seen. He said absolutely nothing to prove his statement which is, obviously, not only unparliamentary but unworthy of a good citizen.
Mr. Speaker, the greatest authority in parliamentary procedure, Erskine May, mentions in the 19th edition, at page 445, that among the most unparliamentary terms, and he lists about thirty, are the words "corrupt" and "corruption". Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, also a well known authority in the matter, states in the fourth edition, at page 130, citation 155 of the English version, that the term "corrupt" is also quite unparliamentary. And again yesterday, when the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) was saying, and I quote from page 6860 of Hansard:

Mr. Speaker, the acts of the minister and the words of the minister have been described as despicable. They could be described as being beneath contempt, they could be described as being vicious and vulgar-
Summer Recess
This expression is forbidden also by Beauchesne's and it is clearly established that "vicious" and "vulgar" are unparliamentary words.

Mr. Speaker, these words of despicable government, of vicious and vulgar words, were spoken by the House leader of the official opposition and are a poor example for the Canadian people who are observing us on television, of the attitude which should prevail in this chamber where we should not criticize individuals and tarnish reputations but rather criticize specific measures and discuss ideas. We should bring the debates in this House to a respectable level, Mr. Speaker, and I think that the attitude of the House leader of the official opposition has not contributed to raising the level of debates during the present session, and I truly regret it. That is the saddest aspect of my experiences as Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council, Mr. Speaker, and it is unfortunate that I should have to say it, and I purposely waited for the hon. House leader of the opposition to be present so that I could tell him to his face.
I noticed that when the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) was laying blame on him that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton left the chamber. I waited for his return to tell him to his face that I am saddened by his attitude. I regret that kind of attitude and I hope that in the future we will be able to work in a more professional way for the good of all Canadians, in a renewed parliament, in a parliament whose procedure will have been amended in good faith in order to be more dignified, more efficient and more adapted to our 1979 life style.

Mr. Speaker, having listened to most of the speeches made since noon today, I have come to the conclusion that we should have adjourned as early as last night. I see that everything that has been said today was not very useful. Usually we wait until much later in the summer before adjourning for the recess, and I think that June 30 is either too soon or too late.
I noticed while listening to the speech of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs that he was very agitated, probably because he has been considerably irritated by the incidents of a few moments before, but whatever the reason, I think that his remarks were somewhat out of place. The minister complained about the proliferation of third parties or of political parties in Canada.
Well, for the minister's information, this is no novel thing in this House, and if third parties sprung up in Canada, it was precisely because of the failure of the older political parties. If they had given Canadians the kind of administration they were expecting from a good government, there would have been no need to create new political parties.

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
The hon. member also suggested that third parties enjoy the same privileges in this House as does the official opposition. I submit this is totally untrue. Time allocations for debates in this House afford much ampler scope to the official opposition, with their greater number of members, than to third parties. On this also I therefore feel the minister twisted the facts when he indicated that third parties enjoyed the same privileges as opposition parties to make their views known. My feeling is that this proportion is "maintained", if not overly "maintained".
The minister also complained that government back-benchers do ask too few questions during question periods, before orders of the day. What he meant in my view was that government members did not participate as much as the opposition parties in that period, considering we are now on television. And my answer to the minister is this: when an opposition member asks a question, he or she gets an answer forthwith or at least the minister tries to answer, and therefore suggest that the ratio is very well maintained because as many government members appear on the screen as opposition members. I note that before TV came into this House, no government members ever rose to ask questions. So, Mr. Speaker, my feeling is the Minister of State for Urban Affairs in his remarks showed much more anger at what happened earlier today than a positive attitude toward improving the debates in this House.
Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members, I have had the opportunity of working under our able Speaker of the House of Commons within a committee which set up the organization for broadcasting and telecasting our debates in the House. This is a new experience which we lived through during this past session, and after having observed the public at least in the area I am representing, and the persons I chanced to meet,
I clearly have the impression that this undertaking is well taken by public. It creates a closer relationship between the Parliament of Canada and the public it represents. It also enables the Canadian public to better understand what goes on in its national parliament.
However, that does not mean that any improvement in the administration is necessarily visible. The performance of the government during the past session is not so much laudable, and I think that the concerns expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there were possibilities of an election in the fall are unjustified because at that time the government would have to go before the people empty-handed. Personally, I rather think that they will try to restore their fortunes during the coming winter months in order to be able to go before the people of Canada with a better image of their administration.
What we have particularly deplored in the last few months is the devaluation of the dollar. In my opinion, this is detrimental for business in Canada, for industry, trade, employment and the cost of living. The whole Canadian economic
[Mr. Laprise.l
system has suffered from the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. And when I look at the present situation in Canada, that is the devaluation of the dollar, an employment level lower than we have seen in a long time, unemployment around 9 or 10 per cent, and even higher in certain areas of the country, a rate of inflation that the government has not succeeded in controlling in spite of all its efforts, when I see these things, Mr. Speaker, this reminds me of the situation which existed in 1960 and 1961 when another administration governed Canada and was defeated because of this. I am talking about the Progressive Conservative government of 1958 to 1962. The same situation existed in 1962 at the time of the general election. The dollar had been devaluated. There was very high unemployment and uncontrollable inflation. We now have the same situation, and perhaps even worse this year, after about 15 years of a Liberal administration.
The government talks about taking all sorts of initiatives to fight against inflation while it takes action which increases the cost of living. It has also taken action to increase every six months, for instance, the cost of oil, gasoline and heating oil in Canada. This increases significantly production and transportation costs and has disastrous effects right down to the level of the distribution of goods and services, and the Canadian consumer must pay for it. The oil price increase serves only to fill the pockets of the multinational companies.
Mr. Speaker, when the government claims it is taking steps to fight inflation, I feel it takes them to increase the cost of living. There is also widespread discontent in the field of agriculture. Dairy producers, be it industrial or raw milk, are clearly dissatisfied with the policy of our government. Nothing has been done to improve and stabilize the Canadian dairy industry. That is sadly lacking and the government should bring forward a long-term policy to stabilize production and especially farm incomes.
In the beef industry, we have erratic fluctuations between highs and lows. Farmers always have a hard time to follow those fluctuations when beef goes through crises such as those we have witnessed in the last two or three years. Instead of suffering terrible losses, farmers get rid of their herds. The herds having been decimated, we see the higher prices we are now experiencing. Now, Mr. Speaker, I feel that once again the government has failed to give leadership by not introducing a policy to stabilize production in those sectors.
Another area on which I want to dwell before concluding my comments-and on this I entirely agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-is that of senior citizens. We have been working and fighting for a long time to obtain from the government more satisfactory pensions for older persons and I refuse to admit more particularly what happens in the case of persons from 60 to 65 years of age, for example, whether they are widows or unmarried persons, but especially widows. Again recently there was in my riding a couple of senior citizens, the wife being under 65 when
June 30, 1978

her husband died. She lost her pension because she was not 65 years old. She became a widow and consequently, under the legislation, she lost her pension. 1 think it is at that time that a person between 60 and 65 badly needs the assistance of the government, because at her age she cannot go back to work. I think that the legislation should be amended as quickly as possible to give justice in such specific cases. I think that the same goes for unmarried persons between 60 and 65 years of age.
Another point too is that of the unfinished business. We might come back in October to continue this session but it might be a new one. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think we will have to consider a draft constitution this summer and parliament will be asked to debate that draft when we come back in the fall.
I think this draft constitution was prepared in a bad approach by the budget debate, mainly as regards the debate on the sales tax. I think the verbal row between the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Quebec minister of finance in particular and other ministers at both levels of government did not help at all that attempt at constitutional amendment. I think that instead of trying to pick a fight all the time, we should try to negotiate in good faith on both sides with a view to arriving at a real constitution that will give satisfaction not only to the province of Quebec, not only to the federal government but also to any and all provinces and nationalities in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, during this holiday period, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested, I think we should rather try to find ways of coming back in the fall better prepared to introduce and pass legislation more in line with the requirements of the people of Canada. As far as I am concerned, I believe, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that this holiday period could have been shorter. We could come back in early September but adjourn a little more often. Instead of adjourning for long periods of three and one third months as is the case now we should adjourn for shorter periods but more often so members would have more opportunities to visit their ridings, meet their voters and know their opinions to be able to represent them better in this House.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I wish all my colleagues of every political party in this House a good holiday and I hope after listening to certain speeches that during that summer period they will be able to have a healthy rest and come back in a better disposition toward agreement than is the case today as we prepare to part.

The hon. member for Leeds.

Mr. Speaker, it is very tempting, after sitting here and listening to the sanctimonious twaddle that originated from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and also to the remark made by the Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) that this has been a positive session-in other words, that we have accomplished something-to take them up on their remarks. But rather than fall for their red herrings that they have tried to place before this House today, it is better to deal with the real issues that face this country.
It is a sad day indeed that we are adjourning this House at a time when the Canadian people need help more than they ever needed it before. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) drew to the attention of the House this morning, and I think it bears repetition, this fact in the form of a question asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Would the member from somewhere out west, I think it is Vancouver-Kingsway, who I hear in the background, cool down? The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) had asked the Prime Minister whether he could tell us when he will announce significant new economic measures to deal with the serious economic problems facing this country. The reply is well worth repeating because nothing has happened. It is obvious nothing will happen and it is obvious that this government is incapable of making anything happen. The Prime Minister made this reply at page 5307 of Hansard:
-the Canadian people are concerned, and they want solutions to these problems at this time. The question arises as to whether these issues can best be dealt with during a general election, or by continuing the work in the House. I have reached the conclusion, because, I must say, of the co-operation of hon. members opposite and their anxiety to get on with the work, that we should stay in this House and deal with these issues.
We stayed and we did not deal with any of these issues.
You should deal with them.

We still have one million people unemployed in this country. We still have the highest inflation that we have ever had in the history of Canada. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, we have the saddest dollar that Canada has ever seen. It reflects on the opinion that others in this world have of this country when the Canadian dollar, even though it has been propped up by billions of dollars by this government over a period of time, still cannot stay at a proper level.

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
It seems to me that the Prime Minister and the government do not care. The backbenchers on the other side obviously do not care either, or they are too scared to do anything about it. The government do not care about the person who is on a pension who goes to the grocery store and cannot afford to pay the prices asked for food today. They do not care about the man without a job who is sitting at home and going out and looking for things that are not there in the way of work, and they do not care about the dollar and the fact that it is a joke in the eyes of the world.
In 1968 we had all of these problems to some extent. Ten years have now gone by since this Prime Minister and this government have been in office, and we still have the same problems. We were told in 1968 that we were going to get a "just society".
Just for Grits.

Our problems became worse. And as has just been said by an hon. member, it is "just for Grits". That is about what it became. Instead of a just society, it has become an unjust society. We were told we would have participatory democracy. What have we had? We have had a Prime Minister who in effect says to this country: "I will allow you to kiss the emperor's feet". We remember too that the Prime Minister said, "Inflation has been licked". At another time he said, "I will wrestle inflation to the ground". It has been a darn poor wrestling match without any results in the interests of the Canadian people. I believe the Prime Minister has been the worst forecaster and the worst prophet in the history of Canada. He has been followed by a bunch of derelict cabinet disciples who do not have the guts to stand up to him and do something about it.
Thank goodness for men like James Richardson-
Order, please. I would like to remind the hon. member that he should refer to a member of this House by his riding and not by his name.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Thank goodness for men like the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson), for those who came before him and for those who I hope will come after him, who have enough sense to get away from a disintegrating, bumbling bunch of people who are incapable of running this country and. are apparently interested in putting ahead of the welfare of this country-
It is despicable.

It is despicable, an hon. member says. The truth hurts, does it not? These people are prepared to put their own political skins ahead of running this country properly.
I remember the Prime Minister making a speech somewhere in western Ontario not many months ago in which he said that Canadians are too concerned with two cars in the yard and a house in the country, and they should pull in their belts. I say what about the two $85,000 Cadillacs and the summer home at Harrington Lake that the taxpayers of this country are

paying for? Is the Prime Minister pulling in his belt as an example? Is he doing away with one of his two Cadillacs? Is he closing Harrington Lake for the duration of the economic crisis of this country? No, he is carrying on saying "Do what I say, but I will do what I want for myself'. What concern for the Canadian people and what an example of practising what is preached. The emperor and his court jesters must go. They must go while there is at least time for something to be left of this country. This heartless piece of stone and his puppets must be and will be disposed of by the Canadian people at the ballot box as soon as there is an opportunity.
Phony.

We have had ten years of failure. Phony, the hon. member says. I reply to her, Mr. Speaker, that the whole record of the government has been phony; it has done nothing for this country in ten years of failure. They deserve a very final reward and that is the judgment of banishment from the treasury benches of this country by the Canadian people.
Speaking of this would-be emperor, for two years he has wiggled and waggled with regard to questions on the order paper, using citations from Beauchesne as though he were the Speaker of the House of Commons. Some of his ministers have taken up the same practice with the result that we get back an answer saying, "See Beauchesne citation number" this or that.
In actual fact, he has no right to usurp the functions of the Speaker, as he is doing. I know he thinks he is important and that he is everything. Once he did say that he was very close to the Almighty. I cannot judge that because none of us is in the position to be that high up the ladder to know whether that is true or not. However, I certainly can say that the Prime Minister is not the Speaker of this House of Commons. The Speaker of the House of Commons is to be commended on the fact that questions are being allowed to be returned to the order paper where the Prime Minister has used Beauchesne's citations to get out of giving an answer.
I do not need to go into the arrogance and disdain for parliament shown by the government. That has often been pointed out by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in such adequate fashion that it would be redundant for me today to go any further in that direction.
I would like to say a word about the Quebec language legislation and the lack of federal government response in a responsible way to such legislation. Next Monday, businesses in Quebec must have French only signs and names. What has our Messiah of the House of Commons, the self-proclaimed protector of minorities, done about it all? He stood in the shadows and whimpered like a scared goat instead of standing up and saying with more than just a few brief words to Rene Levesque that any Canadian has the right to use the language of his choice. He has roared with a whisper. He has wielded nothing but a feather.
Why did he not refer bill 101 to the Supreme Court of Canada for judgment as to whether it was within the rights of
June 30, 1978

the province of Quebec to pass certain sections of that act? Why has he not considered disallowance of such an act? We know why. The obvious answer is a political answer. The answer is politics and votes, which mean more to this government than the supposed protection of the minority rights of any group in this country, whether they be French, English or some other ethnic minority.
Recently the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) spoke across the river in Hull at the opening of a new building. As someone pointed out earlier, they are moving all the departments over there. In any event, he said that when public servants are over there, they should always be sure and speak French. He was telling English Canadians who work in Hull they should not use their own language when they are over there. We do not say to people over there that when they come here they cannot use their language. That would be utterly ridiculous, abominable and a disgrace. Likewise, the words of the Minister of Supply and Services were reprehensible, disgraceful and disgusting. He sounded more like Rene Levesque than a federal member of parliament. He completely illustrated the farce of this government's bilingual program.
When we are told to co-operate, to bend over for the unity of this country, that is what we must do. However, how do the government expect to get an enthusiastic response from the rest of Canada to these sorts of statements when they do not stand up to a government which seeks to separate this country, the government of one particular province which thumbs its nose at the Government of Canada and the Canadian people and everyone who does not speak one particular language? I say that bilingualism "Trudeau style" has become nothing more than two-faced idiocy.
Personally, I am sick and tired of the anti-British and anti-American attitude of this government. Britain gave us our House of Commons. We are modelled on the British parliamentary system.
I found it a bit sickening to listen to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) a while ago saying some things about the British parliamentary tradition. After all, the Prime Minister certainly does not indicate very often that he has very much belief in it. However, when things looked rough in 1972, he rushed over to have tea with the Queen. That was because he almost lost an election, and it looked good to sit on her coat-tails in order to save his own political hide. He has always found time for disrespect for British institutions. He found time to slide down a bannister some years ago. More recently he did a little pirouette behind the Queen, that disrespectful little dance that we saw in all the papers.
This government and the Prime Minister are the greatest manipulators of the century. They are the Houdini of all Houdinis. When it comes to being a Houdini, they attempt to intimidate and manage the press. The Prime Minister managed to grab one of the press members by the coat or the neck a few months ago and started to shake him. He does not want to have much to do with the press until he needs them. When things look a bit shaky for him, they are called in for drinks and interviews. Everything is on the House. He says to
Summer Recess
himself that he needs them and their publicity for election purposes.
I spoke of anti-Americanism. In this regard I wish to refer to a book which I think is well worth reading for all Canadians, "Trudeau Revealed" by David Sommerville. In particular, I refer to page 208. It contains a statement which I recall being made at the time. It was well publicized, although perhaps not well enough. I think it bears repetition now. This is what he said when speaking in the Soviet Union:

Mr. Speaker, when we took our short break for royal assent I was talking about Patrick O'Callaghan, the publisher of the Edmonton Journal, and his comments on the matter of the Toronto Sun and the Peter Worthington case. All that remains to be said in this regard is that his article of June 28 was, to me, a classic example of irresponsible journalism. He showed complete lack of knowledge of the facts and he certainly showed no interest in discovering what really happened before he wrote what he did.
I would like to refer to only two parts of that article where he deals with certain remarks about myself that are not accurate and not true, and I believe he should stand corrected. He said that I hid behind parliamentary privilege. Mr. Speaker, I hide behind nothing on the matter of national security. I was not aware whether or not 1 had privilege. That was a matter that was judged by the law officers of the Crown and subsequently announced in the House by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). I had no advance knowledge of what that judgment would be, and I made up my mind that I would go ahead in the interests of what I thought was right for Canada, regardless of what the judgment might be, and in that regard Mr. O'Callaghan is quite incorrect. Then he says:
Mr. Basford chose not to notice that Mr. Cossitt had also referred to the information in his possession outside the Commons where he has no such protection.
The Minister of Justice did not ignore that fact, and while I do not have his statement in front of me, I recall his saying that he or his law officers had examined what had been said outside the House, that it was substantially and exactly the same as what had been said inside the House. Therefore, again the remarks made by the publisher of the Edmonton Journal are incorrect.
Of course, there are many, many other things in this article that are incorrect, and I suggest that a responsible journalist and publisher should act more in keeping with the position he holds than this man has done, not only in this article but in another one reprinted by the Canadian Daily Newspapers Publishers' Association a few weeks ago.
A few days ago a question put by me on the order paper was answered. It dealt with the Canadian National Railways. I was refused an answer on the grounds "it was not the practice of CN to reveal. .." CNR is owned by the people of Canada. The CBC is owned by the people of Canada. The Canada Council is owned by the people of Canada. As the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) pointed out this morning, there might be around 400 Crown corporations owned by the people of Canada. Why does this parliament not have the right to ask questions about the activities of those corporations and receive answers to them? We are being continually blocked with the expression "it is not the practice to reveal".
Whoever set up these practices should withdraw them and allow democracy to flourish in this country, and freedom of

information, which is being so eloquently espoused by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), should be first and foremost before this parliament. Because when the day comes that a member is not allowed to ask questions as to why we spend, for example, $60,000 of the taxpayers' money on the Factory Theatre Lab in Toronto where they staged a play in which Adolf Eichmann spends some time wiping human excrement on his face, there is something wrong; when we cannot get an answer to a question like that, there is something wrong. When we give public money to people who publish Strike, the tabloid in Toronto, and the Pulp Press of Vancouver who support groups in Italy, such as the terrorists who have been so prominent recently, or those who published a manual called The Urban Guerilla, as was done in Vancouver, there is something wrong. When public money goes to institutions which advocate murder, kidnapping and other acts of a similar nature, and we wish to question that in this parliament but cannot get an answer from the minister responsible for the Crown corporation involved, then something is seriously amiss.
Today we will be going home with the country in a mess, and I think it is shameful. I recall the words spoken by the right hon. member for Prince Albert at the nomination meeting held in my constituency some months ago for the coming election. The theme of his address was, "Where are we going?" That is what every Canadian is asking today. Where are we going? We have not gone anywhere for ten years under this government; our problems have been getting continually worse. The government promised to do something about them before we went home, but it has done nothing, and today all the ministers, with one or two exceptions, have left the House and have probably already gone home. Undoubtedly the Prime Minister has climbed aboard a jet somewhere to fly to some exotic, far-off country, leaving far behind one million unemployed, the poor who suffer from inflation, and the sagging dollar.
The hon. gentleman opposite shakes his head. I know that in all sincerity he must be trying to restrain himself from admitting the truth. But in any event the truth is apparent to the Canadian people. The Prime Minister and his government, who have given us the highest unemployment since the great depression, must go. The Prime Minister and his government, who have permitted the highest inflation in our history, must go. The Prime Minister and his government, whose actions have destroyed the values of the Canadian dollar, must go. Canada needs a breath of fresh air, and if this government calls an election-if it dares or has the nerve to call an election-Canada will get a new government. I am sure no one on the Progressive Conservative side of the House is prepared to say that we will solve all problems, because that would be ridiculous. But at least we know that we will try, and that is more than the government can say. It has not tried for the past ten years.
I am glad the hon. member for Vancouver South has come back. Now she is going out again. She is having a hard time to contain herself.
