That was completely and fully explained in the House. At the same time, the reasons for not proceeding with the charges against other parties were explained. The hon. member for Leeds was one of those people.
The hon. member for Leeds, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) and several others on that side of the House, have expressed from time to time in this place an interest in the welfare of the RCMP and the security of this nation. At the very least one would expect one of those members might have appeared recently at the sittings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, which investigated the estimates of the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), the RCMP and the security directorate of this country. This throttling or preventing of debate apparently occurred in relation to the budget and its associated measures, which debate occurred over four weeks, and upon which many members of the House had spoken. After that passage of time and who knows how many words, the leader of the Tory opposition had the effrontery to attempt to make the case that they had been muzzled and not allowed full comment. Those arguments and the ones we have heard today are about as worthy of credibility as the allegation that certain offices around here had been bugged. They are about as worthy of belief as the unsubstantiated rumours and stories which were floated around the House by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) indicating that members on this side had participated and engaged in a speculation against the dollar.

We know that the allegations by the hon. member for York-Simcoe could not be substantiated. We know how much those people who bugged offices were known on that side of the House. Those comments were about as genuine as the rest of the rumours and bad mouthings on numerous occasions by people of that ilk. As it turned out later, none of them could be substantiated. I should like to refer back to the budget for a moment. My information is that something over 40 members participated in that debate. We on this side of the House, as the government, were accused of throttling debate when we brought in a time allocation measure in order to get on with the business of the House. There were a goodly number of other speakers, mainly opposition members, who spoke on another item, Bill C-48, the measure respecting amendments to the Customs Tariff. That was not the case painted by the Tory party. That was not the case they would have Canadians believe. It was not the case painted by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Continually they make these allegations and indulge in innuendos which are unsubstantiated by fact.
Recently, I am sure by mistake, a pamphlet was delivered to my office. It was a broadsheet entitled: "Leader's Report, Some News From Joe Clark". It was dated May 26, 1978. It referred to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) being "obliged to get on with the governing of the country". It accused the Prime Minister of "political manoeuvring". Also it indicated that the hon. Leader of the Opposition exacted from the Prime Minister a "promise that the government would immediately bring forward specific proposals to deal with the very serious problems now affecting us". In fact, that was repeated by the Tory House leader today.
I should like to continue referring to this despicable little broadsheet. It suggested that the promise was unfulfilled. Supposedly it reprinted the order paper for the House of Commons of May 16. The statement referring to that reads as follows:
"The order paper for the House of Commons of May 16 speaks for itself."
Then it contained the following heading: "Business Disposed of this Week". Following that was a reprint of the portion of the order paper showing specific subject headings and the business conducted. That little pamphlet, which 1 so despise, conveniently left out the fact that May 16 was a Tuesday. No matter what the Tory opposition attempts to do, it cannot change the fact that May 16, 1978 was a Tuesday. In the pamphlet they attempted to make the case that no business was disposed of that week, according to the order paper. They conveniently left out the fact that the business disposed of that "week" does not refer to a five-day week but to a Monday. They very conveniently dropped the fact from that little pamphlet that the statement which is printed in the order paper on May 16 could refer to one day and one day only, Monday. They are trying to sell Monday as the whole of the week, and trying to sell the idea that the government had conducted no business that week because it had done nothing on Monday.
Let us look a little further, Mr. Speaker. It would seem to some that the dropping of the reference to Tuesday, and thus giving the impression that the word "week" meant the whole week rather than just one day, might have been an oversight. That could have been an oversight, but others might just as easily feel that such a slip was more coolly calculated to

deceive. That latter impression might be given some substance by a closer look at the facts.
When one turns to Hansard of May 15 one finds that on that day this House began second reading consideration of Bill C-48. When one looks a little further and makes a little closer examination, one finds there were nine speakers that day on that measure, and of those nine speakers there was one from this side of the House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), there were six Tories, one NDP member and one Creditiste. We have this case of the Tory opposition in their leader's pamphlet trying to sell to the Canadian public and those who buy this sort of garbage that there was nothing done all week, when that reference was to one day. When you look at what was done that one day you find that six Tories spoke, one Liberal, one New Democrat and one Creditiste. One finds in essence, if you look at the facts, that they conveniently overlooked that if there was nothing completed that day, and nothing done in finality, it was not because the government did not put forward any measures, but because the Tories would not or could not stop talking.

Based on all the facts, when everything is looked at, the comments in this report of the Leader of the Opposition fall nothing short of being misleading, distorted and deceiving. One might hope that the Leader of the Opposition would feel some capacity for embarrassment by that happening; that he might stand and withdraw or retract that kind of statement, or at the very least might come clean and correct the erroneous impression that it creates. After all, let us be frank, the Leader of the Opposition in Canada is presumed to have a somewhat higher station in life, and one would not expect from him the kind of statement that is more akin to the kind of thing one expects from some fly by night, door to door huckster.
The reprint from Hansard is, of course, accurate as far as it goes, but the deception arises in what is not said and what is conveniently left out. The Leader of the Opposition acts like a salesman who tells an unsuspecting purchaser of his goods that they are written up in Consumer Affairs, or in Good Housekeeping magazine. That unsuspecting purchaser relies on that statement and buys those goods only to find out that the article in the magazine was a warning not to buy, or that it was one pointing out defects in the product. I hope the people of this country will look hard and long at the kind of statements opposition members have made over the past few months in debate in this House, and at the kind of things being sent to them through the mails. One might ask whether that kind of distorted impression of what goes on in the House went out under the frank of the Leader of the Opposition.
One would hope that the Leader of the Opposition, since he is expected to be an honourable man, is not responsible for that kind of report as it is written. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Or it speaks, as my hon. friend says, with two tongues, so long as they are not bilingual ones.
The opposition House leader today painted a picture of gloom and doom in Canada and how disastrous things are. We have not gone from riches to rags in this country; we are rich. We are not as rich as we hoped we might be at this time, but we are richer than we were. We have had a recession in this country as has almost every other country in the world of late, but the effect of that recession has not been felt in Canada as hard as it has been felt elsewhere. We have managed to cushion the effect of the shock of the recession in this country better than any other country.
No one is going to deny that we have high unemployment in this country today and that it is too high. However, we have not had a decline in the number of people working in this country, as has been seen in the United States, West Germany and Japan. The growth rates in Canada are among the highest of any country in the world and the inflation rates are among the lowest. Canada stands thirty-first in population among the countries of the world. There are only a handful of countries that are more powerful than we are, but they all have twice the population we have. We are an under-populated country yet we have that same power which is relative to those countries that are twice as densely populated as we are.

The most recent World Bank atlas states that Canada has the eighth largest economy in the world and that we are the seventh most productive in the world. It is true that there are some nations like Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar that are ahead of us on this scale, but when people ask why, they find out that those three countries hold that position because they pump a great deal of oil out of the ground. That is the totality of their economy. We stand seventh on that list of countries which are most productive in this world, and the sixth country in the United States. While the attempt on the part of the Tory opposition today was to paint a bad, black and gloomy picture, we are still in good stead as far as the World Bank atlas is concerned.
In the first five months of this year we have created new jobs at an annual rate of 439,000. The profit picture in Canada is improving substantially, as reported to the Conference Board of Canada recently. Our merchandise trade balance is now rolling up healthy surpluses, largely due to the fact that we have a devalued dollar. I do not know any businessman in this country today that is objecting too much to the fact that we have a devalued dollar.
What we have sitting opposite in the House is not an opposition, a group which provides healthy and constructive criticism, but a random cluster of individualists, a cabal of hit and run headline hunters, slippery-tongued salesmen who would be more fitted to selling snake oil medicine at a fly-bynight show. Their talk is all bark and no substance. The fog they throw out to confuse and disillusion the Canadian public disperses with sunlight and a close inspection and examination of the true facts.
I welcome this break. I hope that the opposition will go home, review their mistakes of this past year and come back with an improved performance. I am sure that if we had an improved performance from the opposition, we could also hope to have an improved performance from the government. But let us see it come from that side. We on this side are not afraid of criticism. A good, strong opposition that has something constructive to say will be of benefit to us. We do not mind being prodded or told that we have got work to do; that is fair game and fair comment in this House. Instead of the carping and constant criticism which comes from that side of the House, let us have something of substance, something concrete, something that moves forward and that gets on with doing the job in this House.
Before I close I would like to move-and I understand that this motion may be seconded by a member opposite:
That this sitting continue beyond the ordinary hour of adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of the motion of adjournment before the House in the name of the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council.
That is seconded by me, sir.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought we were enjoying a very fine exchange, my close brother from Newfoundland and I. I do not know why anyone from Cape Breton would interject into a good Scottish exchange. We were having a very good time until he appeared on the scene.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to be deterred by any gusts from the honourable Gus. He may as well subside. Come down from the mountain and subside. I want to get on with my real grievance, the reason I stayed here all day.
My grievance is this. It is on behalf of nine million to ten million taxpayers. In my younger days I had the mistaken and
June 30, 1978

foolish belief that the tax laws of Canada were administered impartially, with equality to all, fairly, and that we were all treated alike in the administration of the tax laws of Canada. In the last two years I have discovered that is not the case.
I have unearthed a scandal of gigantic dimensions involving income tax in Canada. I have managed to piece it together. On May 19 I wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a six page memorandum outlining the situation in connection with John Christopher Doyle. He was a Canadian citizen up to two years ago, when he became a Panamanian citizen in order to avoid extradition to Canada. I sent that memorandum to the Prime Minister on May 19. It sets out what happened in the income tax treatment of Mr. Doyle. It points out that for 1950, 1953 and 1954, the only years made public, that gentleman was re-assessed in the years 1955 and 1959. The Crown added income to his income. In one case, 1950, it was $200,000. In the second case, 1959, it was $1,800,000 and some odd dollars. He was re-assessed like taxpayers are from time to time.
In the normal course of events, as set out in the manuals of the Department of National Revenue, when you are reassessed and tax is found against you in the re-assessment, you have to pay your tax within so many days. Before you appeal, you either have to pay the tax or put up satisfactory security such as a bank guarantee or a bond. In the case of Mr. Doyle, this was not insisted upon. He did not have to put up any security. Because of that, it did not matter to him whether he ever paid the income tax or whether the case ever went to court.
Mr. Doyle put in his notice of appeal. These two cases where he was re-assessed, in 1954 and 1959, were not heard by the Income Tax Appeal Board until 1967, eight years after the re-assessment in the case of the major re-assessment. The Crown did not do anything to move it forward. Therefore it was heard in 1967. An ordinary taxpayer's appeal would have been heard long before that because he would have paid the tax or put up security which was costing him money. It was not costing Doyle anything, and the Crown did not do anything.
Eight years later, the Income Tax Appeal Board heard his appeal. It dismissed the appeal. He appealed to the Exchequer Court of Canada on June 29, 1970. Mr. Justice Gibson dismissed his appeal and reaffirmed the re-assessment for millions of dollars.
On October 15, 1970, Mr. Doyle gave notice of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Crown did nothing for the next seven years to bring that appeal before the Supreme Court of Canada. Naturally Doyle did nothing, because he did not pay his tax. Doyle was not paying for a bond or a bank guarantee. They had not even received any satisfactory security from Doyle. He did not care if it was ever heard.
This man was treated better than all the other taxpayers of Canada. When I raised this matter in the House of Commons a year and a half ago, action finally commenced. One appeal was heard in the fall of 1977. It was dismissed from the bench by the Supreme Court of Canada. They did not have to consider their judgment.
Summer Recess
The second appeal, a major appeal, was heard May 3 and 4, 1978. Twenty-four years after the income tax year in question, it was heard by the Supreme Court of Canada, and dismissed from the bench. They did not hold back their judgment one second. As soon as the lawyers finished, they dismissed the appeal, involving several millions of dollars, with costs to the Crown. There were no unusual points of law involved. There was no unusual difficulty. Why this kind of treatment?
We now discover that $5,014,281.13 is owed by Mr. Doyle for the years 1950, 1953, and 1954. It has not been paid 28 years after 1950, and 24 years after 1954. These amounts still have not been paid. The Crown has not got security. The Crown is now unable to collect on the few shares and share certificates it has because Mr. Doyle and his lawyers are challenging their security. They have not been able to sell or realize a cent.
Mr. Doyle no longer lives in Canada. The same Mr. Doyle has control of 18.4 per cent of the shares of Canadian Javelin Limited, a Canadian company incorporated under the Canadian Companies Act. There are 12,000 shareholders, 75 per cent of them American, and he is denuding that company of its assets without anyone apparently being able to do anything about it.
The Canadian government claims it cannot collect the taxes. When we look at today's paper, what do we see? Canadian Javelin Limited had a meeting yesterday to elect directors. The notice of meeting said that Mr. Doyle had a significant role in the company's management in forming its policies and selecting nominees for election as directors. He controls it because his 18.4 per cent gives him control, there being widely scattered shareholders.
It said that Javelin has offered Mr. Doyle $2.7 million in reimbursement for disbursements he spent in maintaining control of the company. Imagine, his personal expenses of $2.7 million for trying to keep that company under his control are coming out of the assets of that company under this plan of Mr. Doyle and his captive board of directors.
Mr. Doyle is attempting to get an option on 4.2 million shares at $1 each, and they are going to pay him interest on the money he spends to take up the option. In other words, Mr. Speaker, that is the same as a rape victim advancing the person who raped her money to cover his expenses, and giving him a chance to do it over again! It is the most extraordinary proposal ever put to a company. This company is controlled by Mr. Doyle and his tame board. That is what this Canadian company is doing. And this government stands by and does nothing.
Not only is that going ahead, but on January 26 of this year Canadian Javelin announced that it was turning over control of four of its subsidiaries to Pavonia SA, a wholly-owned subsidiary based in Panama City, Panama, where Mr. Doyle lives and has control of the situation.
Javelin is to cancel $17.9 million owed to it by its subsidiaries in exchange for further shares in Pavonia, already a wholly-owned subsidiary of Javelin. This is fraud. Pavonia is a wholly-

owned subsidiary of Javelin, and Javelin is going to cancel $17.9 million in debts owed to it by Pavonia and other subsidiaries in exchange for more shares of Pavonia.
If you own 100 per cent of the company, you cannot own any more of it. How can you cancel what the company owes you in exchange for more shares in that company? However, that is what is happening to Canadian Javelin Limited to get the assets of that company in a company in Panama where Mr. Doyle and his cohorts can complete the despoilation of the company.
Since late 1977, in response to pressure from me, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) has had the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission appoint an investigator into fraudulent acts in Canadian Javelin Limited. On May 17, 1977, an order was obtained from the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission appointing Mr. Fred Sparling as an inspector to inquire into allegations of fraud in connection with the operations of Javelin. There is still no report from Mr. Sparling, mainly because Mr. Doyle and his cohorts in Canadian Javelin Limited are taking legal action to attempt to stop Mr. Sparling from completing his work.
Are the Canadian government and Canadian law helpless? Will the government stand by helpless while this company and its shareholders are despoiled of their assets like this? There have been no dividends paid by that company in the last ten years despite various substantial revenues going into it from Wabash mines royalties. Millions of dollars a year are being taken out for the benefit of Mr. Doyle, and the shareholders receive nothing. This is the person with whom we are dealing.
Some people might say that perhaps Mr. Doyle was such an exemplary citizen that the government wanted to give him every chance in connection with his tax problem, that he was such a great builder of Canada, such a man of character and probity, that the government wanted to bend over backwards to treat him better than all the other taxpayers of Canada. That is not so, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Doyle has been a fugitive from justice in the United States since 1965. He fled the United States because he was convicted of wrongfully sending share certificates through the mails there. The judge sentenced him to three months in jail. He fled the country and has not been back there since.
Since 1965 the government has known that this man was a fugitive from justice in the United States. That year he left Canada. He was on bail, having been charged with certain fraudulent acts, he has since been charged on 408 other counts of wash-trading, and he is now in Panama. He will not come back to Canada. He has changed his citizenship and is now a Panamanian citizen.
The government knew that this taxpayer is not an exemplary Canadian citizen. I have been bringing this matter for a year and a half, now, to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the Minister of National Revenue, and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Finally I wrote to the Prime Minister, the head of the government, a man who

had been minister of justice, and I drew all these facts to his attention and asked him to establish a commission of inquiry. Forty-two days ago I wrote to him. It was on May 19-six weeks ago today. I had a perfunctory acknowledgment from someone in his office, and today I asked the right hon. gentleman a question in this House. I was treated with contempt. The Canadian people were treated with contempt. He did not care whether there was a scandal going on in connection with the administration of the tax laws in Canada. He attempted to pass it off as a mere nothing.
Why should I pay my taxes? Why should the other ten million taxpayers in Canada pay taxes, when people like John C. Doyle do not have to pay, simply because they have influence with the government? What is the explanation for that? The Prime Minister was minister of justice in 1967 and 1968 and this matter was not pursued then, either. There have been seven or eight other ministers in that portfolio since then and still nothing has been done. I have now brought the matter directly to the right hon. gentleman's attention.
Any head of government interested in the equal, impartial and fair administration of the tax laws, any prime minister interested in doing away with any hint or breath of scandal connected with the administration of the tax laws, would appoint a commission immediately to get to the bottom of the affair. At least he would authorize the public accounts committee to investigate the matter, or would authorize some other authority to do it. It is necessary to call witnesses to delve into the matter to find out what has happened and why it happened.
Shares of the Canadian Javelin Company held as security by the Crown were worth $18 in September of 1973. Now they are worth $1.70. The stock of that company is off the Montreal Exchange. It is not allowed on the American exchanges. It has been delisted all over the world. There has been action after action taken against it. It has been scandalously used and misused by Mr. Doyle and his cohorts for 20 years. And the Canadian government appears to be powerless. No one raises a voice against it, except myself and a few others. When we do so we are ignored.
What is wrong with Canada, with the administrators of the law in Canada, and the public conscience of Canada, Mr. Speaker? Something like this goes on, and you cannot even get anyone to take an interest. The press is not interested, the media are not interested, the Prime Minister, the head of the country, is not interested. What is wrong? There is $5 million owed by this one taxpayer, it has been owed since 1954, and nobody gives a hoot. Why should the ladies and gentlemen listening to me now pay their taxes? I suggest we all go on a tax strike if the government fails to act with the utmost rigour.
Another thing I want to know, Mr. Speaker, is about the other tax years. The years I refer to are 1954 to 1977. The Minister of National Revenue refuses to give me any information on these years. I am told that is privileged information. What about the fact that in 1964 an attachment was put against Canadian Javelin, the effect of which was to have anything owed to Mr. Doyle paid over to the government?

Then they stood by until the fall of 1977, and ignored the fact that Canadian Javelin failed to comply with the attachment and paid out to Mr. Doyle a million and a half dollars through a company in the Bahamas. They paid the money to Javelin Exports Limited in the Bahamas and Javelin Exports would pay Doyle-all the money coming from Canadian Javelin. This was done in defiance of the government's attachment of 1964, and nothing was done about it. Nothing was done in the ensuing 13 years until I got after them.
The whole thing reeks of influence, of political skullduggery and corruption. We want to see an inquiry established and to know how this happened. What instructions were given to ministers? When were reports of these matters made to ministers? What did those ministers say when it was reported to them down through the years?
As I say, I wrote the Prime Minister a memorandum. It was six pages in length, and I do not have time to read it all into the record. To put this matter in its best light, Mr. Speaker, is to call it willful and wanton misconduct. But I suspect it is really much worse than that. Mr. Doyle has been a Liberal and has been involved on the fringes of the Liberal party for many, many years. He was an intimate of Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland who interceded on his behalf in Ottawa many times. If we ever get a look at those files we shall see that Doyle was an intimate of Mr. Smallwood, an intimate of Mr. Pickersgill. I believe even the Prime Minister knows him. He was involved in Quebec politics for years.
Some books-and I might mention volume III of the memoirs of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert- referred to certain activities which took place in 1963 when a change of government took place in this country. There is a lot under the surface in connection with this matter, Mr. Speaker. We will never know, of course, just what is behind it until the government agrees to hold a proper investigation. I really hope that if an investigation is held it will find there is no corruption, that there is nothing to be discovered and that it is all above board. But I must say that, even if there is no corruption, there is monumental incompetence, the worst kind of negligence, and the worst kind of malfeasance in office.
I asked a question of the Minister of National Revenue the other day and in his reply he told me that there are 14 people in Canada who owe over one million dollars in income tax, as at March 31. One of them owes over $5 million. That is brother Doyle. I am told that the average amount owed by some 613,000 taxpayers is $846. I guess Mr. Doyle really brings that average up with his debt of over $5 million. That is the kind of information I can get from the department, but no information is available to me for the years 1954 to 1977.
Other information I have been unable to obtain concerns how many people put up bank guarantees when they appeal, how many have to pay their taxes, and so on. But in the annual report which comes before this House it is said that the taxpayer has to pay up every time he is reassessed. I quote from that report:
Summer Recess
It has been the practice of National Revenue that taxes assessed against a taxpayer must be paid whether or not there is an objection or an appeal by the taxpayer.
In this connection I refer to the Annual Report of the Department of National Revenue entitled "Inside Taxation", page 40. It states:
During appeal periods the amount assessed must be paid whether or not there is an objection or appeal outstanding. In certain circumstances the department may accept collateral security for the amount of the debt until the issue is resolved.
As a member of this House, I brought this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister thinking, in my foolish innocence, that the Prime Minister of the country would be interested in the fair and proper administration of the tax laws. I thought he would be interested in making sure that any allegation I have set out in my memorandum is wrong. As can be seen from a glance at the right hon. gentleman's answers in Hansard today, he does not care, just as he does not care, in my opinion, about national unity except in a partisan sense; just as the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) does not care about national unity but will use any kind of skullduggery, thuggery and skuggery to try to keep in office, even to the extent of suggesting that members of this House are racially biased.
Are the people of Canada prepared to tolerate this kind of stinking mess the government will not make any attempt to find out about? If there was one thing I always thought, Mr. Speaker, it was that taxpayers were always treated alike. Yet here we have definite proof, beyond any doubt, that taxpayers are not treated equally. One powerful taxpayer with dozens of lawyers in his employ has been able to go for 28 years without paying his taxes. For the last 15 of those years the party opposite has been in power, and for the last ten of them the government has been headed by the Prime Minister. Why is this so? The whole matter cries for a complete public investigation of our tax system, how our taxes are imposed, how they are collected, what security is taken when the Crown reassesses you. The whole thing has to come under the most open kind of scrutiny. There is something wrong with our laws when a company such as Javelin can be raped and raped again, its assets taken out of the country and given over to Mr. John C. Doyle in the Bahamas, in Panama, in Costa Rica, and its shareholders helpless to do anything about it. Twelve thousand shareholders own a few hundred shares each, and there are no major shareholders. It has a captive and subservient board.
Our laws have got to be changed, Mr. Speaker. We can do better than this. A year ago last May the inspector was appointed, and Mr. Doyle has him tied up in court. I have one of the judgments here today, and Mr. Doyle has got other actions going on in Montreal to prevent the government from selling the few scrawny shares they have got in Canadian Javelin, that he owns, to try to collect some of the tax that he owes. Mr. Speaker, that's why I wanted to speak on the adjournment debate, because when we adjourn this is the time to bring forward grievances, and I would like the parliamen-

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
tary secretary or whoever is there from the government to get on to the Prime Minister and say to him, whether this gets much publicity now or doesn't get much publicity now, that the member who is speaking here today is going to keep at it for the next 50 years, if necessary. So it is going to get publicity.
It is going to be in the history books. It is going to be on the record. It is going to come out, and it is better for the Prime Minister to get at it now and appoint an investigation and cut out this canker and this sore.
I am surprised that the national press and media care nothing about it. I sent them copies of all this stuff, and there wasn't a word. The crusading press, the investigatory press, they don't care. They don't care about something like this. Nobody has taken the time and effort to try to go further. I haven't got the resources, Mr. Speaker, to go any further than I have gone. I have done all I can with the resources I have at my command.
And then there is the suggestion about parliamentary immunity. That is a silly argument that was brought forward that we shouldn't have parliamentary immunity. Why, Mr. Speaker, do you think I would dare say anything about these things if we didn't have parliamentary immunity? The people I am dealing with would have me sued from one end of the country to the other. They would be throwing suits-false ones-but I would have to defend myself. I would have to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees even to mention these things. That is what they are doing now with the government. It is going to cost the government hundreds of thousands of dollars to deal with Doyle and his lawyers, preventing them from selling the bit of security they've got, preventing this Mr. Sparling from doing his job. They have got suit after suit.
They are appealing the judgment they just lost against Mr. Sparling in Montreal, now. Lask week the judge found in favour of the government, and the Javelin forces are now appealing that. There is a second case they have taken. Harassment after harassment! He is taking the money from Canadian Javelin, from the other shareholders, from the other 82 per cent. Their money is being used to finance these suits in the hundreds of thousands and millions all over the world, and we are powerless to do anything. So I am glad I have parliamentary immunity, Mr. Speaker. I need it, or I would be frightened to death to open my mouth about this because it would be costing me hundreds of thousands in legal fees.
Don't say that we should take away parliamentary immunity. How are we going to raise the things, Mr. Speaker, if we do not have some kind of immunity? It is not whether you can prove it or not. It is whether you have got the financial assets to go into court on the harassing lawsuits that they would have against you all over the world. I know whereof I am speaking with this gentleman, and I know the tactics they are capable of, and I know the lengths to which they will stoop. But I am dedicated, Mr. Speaker, to getting this resolved one way or the other.
I have lots of other things I am going to do, too, but I have been in this now for the last two years, and as long as I am returned to this House, if we don't have the government-if we have the government there will be a fantastic investigation, you can bet your bottom dollar-if we don't have the government, I will be back at it next year and the year after that, and the year after that. I will be at it as long as I am returned, and that may be a long time. And then if I am not returned, I will still be at it some other way, because, Mr. Speaker, this cries out for investigation.
Why should the little taxpayer of Canada, the man who pays the thousand, the man who pays five thousand, the man who pays ten-and as a lawyer I have come across many cases where they have reassessed you, and they have come in without any compunction, and you pay up what they have reassessed or they put the sheriff right on your assets. They grab your bank account. They put attachments with your employer. Yet there is this rogue and scoundrel, not only despoiling a Canadian company and its 12,000 shareholders, Mr. Speaker, but being treated with kid gloves. He doesn't have to pay the tax, doesn't have to put up adequate security, yet everybody else does. I have seen cases myself where there are tens of thousands of dollars involved, and you had to get a bank guarantee and pay the bank a fee to get the bank guarantee before you were allowed to put in your appeal.
So, Mr. Speaker, there is something wrong here, and I wouldn't be speaking on the adjournment today if the Prime Minister hadn't tried to treat this so lightly. If he knew nothing about it he should have said, "I know nothing about this." Well, it is a serious question here of our income tax, and I am certainly going to get to the bottom of this.
This is the kind of thing you would expect. This is a man I voted for in 1968 to become leader of the Liberal party. My God, how I have been disillusioned, Mr. Speaker. When I first got elected here 20 months ago, I still had a good regard for the man, but from what I have seen in here in the last few months, my regard for him is diminishing quickly, and today put the kibosh on it all together. I thought he was using this national unity bit and so on in a non-partisan manner. I now have got other observations on that, and when we get into the constitutional debate, you bet I am going to lay on the line what I think about that grabbag of constitutional proposals that the Prime Minister has put before us, what I think of them, and what he is up to there. I could give him the benefit of the doubt on that, but now, Mr. Speaker, on this I can't give him the benefit of the doubt.
The man knows better than that. The man has to know better, if he is the Prime Minister. He has been minister of justice of this country, but he tries to cover up and slough me off with his foolish comments on a question like this. So I just leave, Mr. Speaker, and I hope this is the last session of this House. I hope we get to the electorate in the fall or whenever, before we come back here on October 10, but if we don't, I'll be back to ask the Prime Minister about this case, in case my letter is not answered. It is six weeks now. October 10 will be another three or four months, but on October 11, I'll be here

I am not going to let it drop, so the Prime Minister better get on the job and find out just why, for the last ten years, this case has been treated so partially and why one John Christopher Doyle, now a Panamanian citizen, has been given every possible leeway that the human mind could imagine while the rest of the Canadian taxpayers are being bled to death, and stamped on, and seized in the tax, and their assets taken to pay for the debts of this government.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this adjournment debate. I do not know that I have enjoyed the last year or so as much as I would have hoped. There has been much discussion about the RCMP and the Official Secrets Act. There have been scandals here and there, but they all seemed to amount to rather small things. I do not think the public is particularly taken. I think the public has faith in its institutions and will continue to do so.
I was rather pleased today when at the beginning of this debate the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) spoke about economic matters. I do not feel that these matters have been given the attention they should be given. I do not find myself in agreement with the substance of the remarks of the hon. member, but I am certainly pleased that he raised the matter of our economic problems.
One of our economic problems has to do with unemployment. I do not think there is any question that in Canada we have a serious unemployment problem. The hon. member stated that we have the worst unemployment rate of any of the industrial countries. This may be true. I am not sure that I entirely agree with him, but it is probably true on the basis of some of the figures we have, although I have seen some work done about Sweden and other countries and I saw a report last year, which I think was seriously done, which showed that the Swedish unemployment rate at the end of last year was something in the order of 11 per cent.
This comes about partly because people do different things with their unemployed. I am told, for example, that the Japanese unemployment rate, if the Japanese dealt with their unemployed the way we do, would also be very high. Apparently in Japan you do not fire redundant employees, you keep them on. These are some of the things we have to take into consideration. So 1 do not agree entirely with what the hon. member said. I think the unemployment rate is far too high, but I think we should go into it in a little more depth than did the hon. member, and this is what I would like to do for the next three or four minutes. I will keep my remarks very short.
The basic reason we have such a high unemployment rate in this country, maybe higher than in many other countries, has to do with the growth of the labour force. I have a chart here prepared by Statistics Canada which was produced in the last couple of weeks in a publication on this matter. I would like to refer to this chart to give some indication of the increase in the labour force in Canada which has given rise to this very high
Summer Recess
unemployment rate. If you take the base figure of 100 in 1965, we see that in West Germany for every 100 people employed in 1965 there are now only 96 people employed. If we look at Italy, for every 100 people employed in 1965, there are still 100 employed. If we go to the United Kingdom, the figure is now 104 people. In France it is 110, in Sweden it is about 112, in Japan it is about 114. If we go to the United States, for every 100 people on the labour force in 1965 there are now 129. In Australia the number is 130. If we go to Canada, on the other hand, for every 100 people in the labour force in 1965, in 1977 there were 146. This is a very significant figure. Our labour force has grown at a much faster rate than anyone else's.
This is a selection of countries, but I do not know of any other country which would change this picture in the industrialized world. I am giving all of the countries that were listed in this chart; I am not taking one out and adding another one. This is the way this information is produced by Statistics Canada. I think it is extremely important to note that we have 146 people in the labour force today for every 100 we had in 1965, and nobody else comes close to that, not even Australia with 130.
Let us compare Canada with the United States. This is a comparison which we should be looking at partly because 70 per cent of our imports come from the United States and the United States is our major trading nation, so what happens in the United States also happens to us. I think it is important that we look at the United States to see how they fare in this situation. As I indicated, they had 128 people in the labour force in 1977 as opposed to 100 in 1965. If we had the same growth in the labour force as the United States has had, we would have far more jobs than we have people to fill the jobs. I think that is a very important point to remember.
I have other figures which I do not have here, but I would like to give some indication of why this came about. From 1951 to 1971-these are the only figures I have-the school population from grade one to university increased by 240 per cent, two and a half times. At the same time, the population of this country went up by only 30 per cent. There is a factor of eight; the school population grew eight times as fast as the general population. Part of the reason is that people stay in school longer, but one of the other major factors is that we have far more people going into school. I do not have the figures for the United States, but they are much lower than this.
When one condemns the economic situation in this country, it is important to understand how extremely difficult it has been to solve this problem. Admittedly, at a growth rate of 8.5 per cent, an unemployment rate of 8.6 per cent is not desirable; it is far too much. But on the other hand, there are some very strong reasons why we have this problem and we have done a remarkable job in job creation. As one hon. member mentioned earlier, in the first five months of this year the rate was over 450,000 jobs created put on a yearly basis. So we have done a superb job in this situation though we still have a major job to do.

June 30, 1978
Summer Recess
I would like to indicate that I think this is a global situation, it cannot just be seen as the Canadian situation. I will conclude by listing the three factors involved. The first one is that, globally, there has been a quantum leap in the problems that all governments have had to face, such as inflation, unemployment, foreign exchange problems, et cetera. Second, there has been a massive shift in terms of energy problems. We now have a unique notion, that is scarcity, which has created a series of other problems. Third, the techniques that we have traditionally used to solve these problems, Keynesian types of techniques, do not work either because the problems are too large for that kind of solution.
I should like to say in conclusion that we have many problems in this country, but if we are going to solve them, we will have to work together over the next several years as a nation to eliminate them.

Mr. Speaker, there are a couple of matters that I would like to raise on a point of order before the question is put on the motion. The first one has to do with questions on the order paper. I understand that there will be willingness to allow us to deal with questions on the order paper prior to the adjournment motion coming into effect. That is certainly agreeable to us.
The second matter is the discussion which has been going on between the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) with respect to the report of the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments to the effect that the report be allowed to stand rather than be proceeded with in any other way. I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary to consider whether we could do that before we close.
Finally, I understand that today is the last day on which parliament will be served by pages. I have come to know those pages-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has known them for many years before me-and they have served us so well. I understand we may well be proceeding to another system which you, sir, mentioned a few weeks ago.
I thought it might be appropriate if, before we rose-in the event that we will not be back in this parliament-I called the attention of the House to this day being the termination of a particular kind of service by a devoted section of the staff of the House of Commons, and to compliment them on behalf of all members of the House for the work they have done and the devoted service they have rendered to each one of us, sometimes far beyond that which we would normally ask anyone to do except in their most unusual form of service to a most unusual institution.
I would like to say that on behalf of my own party certainly and, I hope, on behalf of all of us in parliament, and to thank those who are here, and those who have gone before them who are represented by those who are here, for their years of devoted service to this parliament, to making it a much better place in which all of us can function.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: Order, please. I should like to make a few comments respecting the pages who were mentioned in glowing terms, quite appropriately.
